Two households, both alike in dignity, / In fair Verona, where we lay our scene, / From ancient grudge break to new mutiny, / Where civil blood makes civil hands unclean. / From forth the fatal loins of these two foes / A pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life; / Whose misadventur'd piteous overthrows / Doth with their death bury their parents' strife. / The fearful passage of their death-mark'd love, / And the continuance of their parents' rage, / Which, but their children's end, nought could remove, / Is now the two hours' traffic of our stage; / The which, if you with patient ears attend, / What here shall miss, our toil shall strive to mend.

Two families, equal in rank and status, live in beautiful Verona, where our play is set. An old feud between them breaks out into new violence, and citizens stain their hands with the blood of fellow citizens. From the deadly bodies of these two enemies come a pair of lovers, crossed by the stars, whose unlucky and pitiful downfall buries their parents' feud along with them. The terrible course of their doomed love, and their parents' continuing anger, which nothing but their children's deaths could end, is what our stage will show for the next two hours. If you listen patiently, whatever we have failed to explain here, our work on stage will try to make good.
Gregory, on my word, we'll not carry coals.
Gregory, I swear, we won't put up with insults.
No, for then we should be colliers.
No, because then we'd be coal-carriers.
I mean, if we be in choler, we'll draw.
I mean, if we get angry, we'll draw our swords.
Ay, while you live, draw your neck out o' the collar.
Yes, and while you're alive, keep your neck out of the hangman's collar.
I strike quickly when I'm provoked.
But thou art not quickly moved to strike.
But you're not quickly provoked into striking.
A dog of the house of Montague moves me.
Any dog from the Montague household provokes me.
To move is to stir; and to be valiant is to stand: therefore, if thou / art moved, thou runn'st away.
To be provoked is to move, and to be brave is to stand still. So if you're provoked, you run away.
A dog of that house shall move me to stand. / I will take the wall of any man or maid of Montague's.
A dog from that household will provoke me to stand and fight. I'll take the safe side of the street, next to the wall, from any Montague man or woman.
That shows thee a weak slave, for the weakest goes to the wall.
That shows you're a weakling: the weakest get pushed to the wall.
True, and therefore women, being the weaker vessels, are ever thrust to / the wall: therefore I will push Montague's men from the wall, and / thrust his maids to the wall.
True, and that's why women, being the weaker sex, always get pushed against the wall. So I'll push Montague's men away from the wall and push his women up against it.
The quarrel is between our masters and us their men.
The quarrel is between our masters, and between us, their men.
'Tis all one, I will show myself a tyrant: when I have fought with the / men I will be civil with the maids, I will cut off their heads.
It's all the same. I'll be a tyrant: when I've fought the men I'll be gentle with the girls. I'll cut off their heads.
Ay, the heads of the maids, or their maidenheads; take it in what sense / thou wilt.
Yes, the girls' heads, or their virginity. Take it whichever way you like.
They must take it in sense that feel it.
The ones who feel it will have to take it in the sense they feel it.
Me they shall feel while I am able to stand: and 'tis known I am a / pretty piece of flesh.
They'll feel me as long as I can stand up, and everyone knows I'm a fine piece of flesh.
'Tis well thou art not fish; if thou hadst, thou hadst been poor John. / Draw thy tool; here comes of the house of Montagues.
Just as well you're not fish, or you'd be dried salt cod. Draw your weapon: here come two of the Montague household.
My naked weapon is out: quarrel, I will back thee.
My sword is out. Pick a quarrel and I'll back you up.
How? Turn thy back and run?
What? Turn your back and run?
No, indeed: I'm worried you'll run!
Let us take the law of our sides; let them begin.
Let's keep the law on our side: let them start it.
I will frown as I pass by, and let them take it as they list.
I'll frown at them as I go by, and they can take it however they like.
Nay, as they dare. I will bite my thumb at them, which is disgrace to / them if they bear it.
No, however they dare. I'll bite my thumb at them, which is an insult they'll be shamed by if they put up with it.
Do you bite your thumb at us, sir?
Are you biting your thumb at us, sir?
I do bite my thumb, sir.
I am biting my thumb, sir.
Do you bite your thumb at us, sir?
Are you biting your thumb at us, sir?
Is the law of our side if I say ay?
Is the law on our side if I say yes?
No sir, I do not bite my thumb at you, sir; but I bite my thumb, sir.
No, sir, I'm not biting my thumb at you, sir. But I am biting my thumb, sir.
Are you trying to pick a fight, sir?
But if you do, sir, I am for you. I serve as good a man as you.
But if you are, sir, I'm ready for you. My master is as good as yours.
Say better; here comes one of my master's kinsmen.
Say 'better': here comes one of our master's relatives.
Draw, if you be men. Gregory, remember thy washing blow.
Draw, if you're men. Gregory, remember your smashing stroke.
Part, fools! put up your swords, you know not what you do.
Break it up, you fools! Put your swords away; you don't know what you're doing.
What, art thou drawn among these heartless hinds? / Turn thee Benvolio, look upon thy death.
What, have you drawn your sword among these cowardly servants? Turn round, Benvolio, and look at your death.
I do but keep the peace, put up thy sword, / Or manage it to part these men with me.
I'm only keeping the peace. Put away your sword, or use it to help me separate these men.
What, drawn, and talk of peace? I hate the word / As I hate hell, all Montagues, and thee: / Have at thee, coward.
What, sword drawn and talking about peace? I hate that word as I hate hell, all Montagues and you. Here I come, coward.
Clubs, bills and partisans! Strike! Beat them down! / Down with the Capulets! Down with the Montagues!
Clubs, spears and axes! Strike! Beat them down! Down with the Capulets! Down with the Montagues!
What noise is this? Give me my long sword, ho!
What's this noise? Give me my long sword, there!
A crutch, a crutch! Why call you for a sword?
A crutch, you need a crutch! Why ask for a sword?
My sword, I say! Old Montague is come, / And flourishes his blade in spite of me.
My sword, I said! Old Montague is here, waving his blade to spite me.
Thou villain Capulet! Hold me not, let me go.
You villain, Capulet! Don't hold me back, let me go.
Thou shalt not stir one foot to seek a foe.
You won't move one step towards an enemy.

Rebellious subjects, enemies to peace, / Profaners of this neighbour-stained steel,— / Will they not hear? What, ho! You men, you beasts, / That quench the fire of your pernicious rage / With purple fountains issuing from your veins, / On pain of torture, from those bloody hands / Throw your mistemper'd weapons to the ground / And hear the sentence of your moved prince. / Three civil brawls, bred of an airy word, / By thee, old Capulet, and Montague, / Have thrice disturb'd the quiet of our streets, / And made Verona's ancient citizens / Cast by their grave beseeming ornaments, / To wield old partisans, in hands as old, / Canker'd with peace, to part your canker'd hate. / If ever you disturb our streets again, / Your lives shall pay the forfeit of the peace. / For this time all the rest depart away: / You, Capulet, shall go along with me, / And Montague, come you this afternoon, / To know our farther pleasure in this case, / To old Free-town, our common judgement-place. / Once more, on pain of death, all men depart.

Rebels against the peace, who dirty your swords with your neighbours' blood! Won't they listen? You there, you men, you beasts, who put out the fire of your deadly anger with fountains of blood from your veins: on pain of torture, throw your misused weapons from your bloody hands to the ground and hear the judgement of your angry prince. Three street fights, started by a careless word, by you, old Capulet, and you, Montague, have three times disturbed the peace of our streets. They have made Verona's old citizens put aside their dignified clothes and pick up old spears in old hands, rusty from peace, to break up your festering hatred. If you ever disturb our streets again, you will pay for breaking the peace with your lives. For now, everyone else, leave. You, Capulet, will come with me; and Montague, you come this afternoon to the old Free-town, our public court, to hear what else I decide in this case. Once more, on pain of death, everyone go.
Who set this ancient quarrel new abroach? / Speak, nephew, were you by when it began?
Who started this old quarrel up again? Tell me, nephew, were you here when it began?

Here were the servants of your adversary / And yours, close fighting ere I did approach. / I drew to part them, in the instant came / The fiery Tybalt, with his sword prepar'd, / Which, as he breath'd defiance to my ears, / He swung about his head, and cut the winds, / Who nothing hurt withal, hiss'd him in scorn. / While we were interchanging thrusts and blows / Came more and more, and fought on part and part, / Till the Prince came, who parted either part.

Your enemy's servants and yours were already fighting hand to hand before I got here. I drew my sword to separate them, and at that moment the hot-headed Tybalt arrived with his sword ready. While he shouted insults at me he swung it about his head and cut the air, which, unharmed, hissed at him in contempt. While we were exchanging thrusts and blows, more and more people came and fought on one side or the other, until the Prince arrived and separated both sides.
O where is Romeo, saw you him today? / Right glad I am he was not at this fray.
Oh, where is Romeo? Have you seen him today? I'm very glad he wasn't in this fight.

Madam, an hour before the worshipp'd sun / Peer'd forth the golden window of the east, / A troubled mind drave me to walk abroad, / Where underneath the grove of sycamore / That westward rooteth from this city side, / So early walking did I see your son. / Towards him I made, but he was ware of me, / And stole into the covert of the wood. / I, measuring his affections by my own, / Which then most sought where most might not be found, / Being one too many by my weary self, / Pursu'd my humour, not pursuing his, / And gladly shunn'd who gladly fled from me.

Madam, an hour before the sun rose, a troubled mind drove me out for a walk, and in the grove of sycamore trees west of the city I saw your son out walking so early. I went towards him, but he saw me and slipped away into the cover of the wood. Judging his feelings by my own, which wanted to be where no one else was, since even my own company was one too many, I followed my mood and not him, and was glad to avoid someone who was glad to avoid me.

Many a morning hath he there been seen, / With tears augmenting the fresh morning's dew, / Adding to clouds more clouds with his deep sighs; / But all so soon as the all-cheering sun / Should in the farthest east begin to draw / The shady curtains from Aurora's bed, / Away from light steals home my heavy son, / And private in his chamber pens himself, / Shuts up his windows, locks fair daylight out / And makes himself an artificial night. / Black and portentous must this humour prove, / Unless good counsel may the cause remove.

He has often been seen there in the mornings, adding his tears to the fresh dew and more clouds to the clouds with his deep sighs. But as soon as the cheerful sun starts to open the curtains of the dawn in the far east, my gloomy son creeps home away from the light, shuts himself up in his room, closes the windows, locks out the daylight and makes himself an artificial night. This mood will turn out dark and dangerous unless good advice can remove its cause.
My noble uncle, do you know the cause?
My noble uncle, do you know the cause?
I neither know it nor can learn of him.
I don't know it, and I can't get it out of him.
Have you importun'd him by any means?
Have you pressed him about it in any way?

Both by myself and many other friends; / But he, his own affections' counsellor, / Is to himself—I will not say how true— / But to himself so secret and so close, / So far from sounding and discovery, / As is the bud bit with an envious worm / Ere he can spread his sweet leaves to the air, / Or dedicate his beauty to the sun. / Could we but learn from whence his sorrows grow, / We would as willingly give cure as know.

Both myself and many other friends. But he keeps his feelings to himself, and is so secretive and closed (I won't say how wisely) and so hard to fathom, that he's like a bud bitten by a spiteful worm before it can open its sweet petals to the air or offer its beauty to the sun. If we could only find out where his sorrows come from, we'd be as glad to cure them as to know them.
See, where he comes. So please you step aside; / I'll know his grievance or be much denied.
Look, here he comes. Please step aside; I'll find out what's wrong, or he'll have to refuse me many times.
I would thou wert so happy by thy stay / To hear true shrift. Come, madam, let's away,
I hope you're lucky enough, by staying, to hear him confess the truth. Come, madam, let's go.
Ay me, sad hours seem long. / Was that my father that went hence so fast?
Oh dear, sad hours seem long. Was that my father who left in such a hurry?
It was. What sadness lengthens Romeo's hours?
It was. What sadness makes Romeo's hours so long?
Not having that which, having, makes them short.
Not having the thing that, if I had it, would make them short.
Out of her favour where I am in love.
Out of favour with the woman I love.
Alas that love so gentle in his view, / Should be so tyrannous and rough in proof.
It's a pity that love, which looks so gentle, should turn out so cruel and harsh when you try it.

Alas that love, whose view is muffled still, / Should, without eyes, see pathways to his will! / Where shall we dine? O me! What fray was here? / Yet tell me not, for I have heard it all. / Here's much to do with hate, but more with love: / Why, then, O brawling love! O loving hate! / O anything, of nothing first create! / O heavy lightness! serious vanity! / Misshapen chaos of well-seeming forms! / Feather of lead, bright smoke, cold fire, sick health! / Still-waking sleep, that is not what it is! / This love feel I, that feel no love in this. / Dost thou not laugh?

It's a pity that love, who is always blindfolded, can still find ways to get what he wants without eyes! Where shall we eat? Oh no! What fight happened here? No, don't tell me, I've heard all about it. This has a lot to do with hate, but more to do with love. So then: oh fighting love! Oh loving hate! Oh something created out of nothing! Oh heavy lightness, serious silliness, ugly chaos made of beautiful shapes! Feather made of lead, bright smoke, cold fire, sick health, sleep that's always awake, that isn't what it is! That's the love I feel, though I feel no love returned. Aren't you laughing?
At how your kind heart is weighed down.

Why such is love's transgression. / Griefs of mine own lie heavy in my breast, / Which thou wilt propagate to have it prest / With more of thine. This love that thou hast shown / Doth add more grief to too much of mine own. / Love is a smoke made with the fume of sighs; / Being purg'd, a fire sparkling in lovers' eyes; / Being vex'd, a sea nourish'd with lovers' tears: / What is it else? A madness most discreet, / A choking gall, and a preserving sweet. / Farewell, my coz.

Well, that's what love does wrong. My own griefs lie heavy in my chest, and you'll add to them by pressing yours on top. The love you've shown me only adds more grief to the too much I have already. Love is a smoke made from the steam of sighs. When it clears, it's a fire sparkling in lovers' eyes; when it's frustrated, it's a sea fed by lovers' tears. What else is it? A very sensible madness, a choking poison and a healing sweetness. Goodbye, cousin.
Soft! I will go along: / And if you leave me so, you do me wrong.
Wait! I'll come with you. If you leave me like this, you're treating me badly.
Tut! I have lost myself; I am not here. / This is not Romeo, he's some other where.
Oh, I've lost myself; I'm not here. This isn't Romeo: he's somewhere else.
Tell me in sadness who is that you love?
Tell me seriously, who is it you love?
What, shall I groan and tell thee?
What, shall I groan and tell you?
Groan! Why, no; but sadly tell me who.
Groan? Why, no. But tell me seriously who.
Bid a sick man in sadness make his will, / A word ill urg'd to one that is so ill. / In sadness, cousin, I do love a woman.
Telling a sick man to make his will seriously is a word badly chosen for someone so ill. Seriously, cousin, I love a woman.
I aim'd so near when I suppos'd you lov'd.
I guessed that much when I supposed you were in love.
A right good markman, and she's fair I love.
A very good marksman! And the woman I love is beautiful.
A right fair mark, fair coz, is soonest hit.
A beautiful target, cousin, is the easiest to hit.

Well, in that hit you miss: she'll not be hit / With Cupid's arrow, she hath Dian's wit; / And in strong proof of chastity well arm'd, / From love's weak childish bow she lives uncharm'd. / She will not stay the siege of loving terms / Nor bide th'encounter of assailing eyes, / Nor ope her lap to saint-seducing gold: / O she's rich in beauty, only poor / That when she dies, with beauty dies her store.

Well, there you miss. She won't be hit by Cupid's arrow: she has the wisdom of Diana, goddess of chastity, and armed with a strong defence of chastity she lives unharmed by love's weak, childish bow. She won't put up with a siege of loving words, or meet the attack of loving looks, or open her lap to gold that would tempt a saint. Oh, she is rich in beauty, and poor only because when she dies, her riches will die with her.
Then she hath sworn that she will still live chaste?
So she has sworn to stay a virgin for ever?

She hath, and in that sparing makes huge waste; / For beauty starv'd with her severity, / Cuts beauty off from all posterity. / She is too fair, too wise; wisely too fair, / To merit bliss by making me despair. / She hath forsworn to love, and in that vow / Do I live dead, that live to tell it now.

She has, and by saving herself she wastes a fortune. Beauty starved by her strictness cuts beauty off from all future generations. She is too beautiful, too wise, too wisely beautiful, to earn heaven by making me despair. She has sworn never to love, and because of that vow I live as a dead man who only lives to tell you about it.
Be rul'd by me, forget to think of her.
Take my advice: forget about her.
O teach me how I should forget to think.
Oh, teach me how to forget to think!
By giving liberty unto thine eyes; / Examine other beauties.
By letting your eyes wander freely. Look at other beauties.

'Tis the way / To call hers, exquisite, in question more. / These happy masks that kiss fair ladies' brows, / Being black, puts us in mind they hide the fair; / He that is strucken blind cannot forget / The precious treasure of his eyesight lost. / Show me a mistress that is passing fair, / What doth her beauty serve but as a note / Where I may read who pass'd that passing fair? / Farewell, thou canst not teach me to forget.

That's the way to make me think even more about how exquisite she is. The lucky black masks that touch ladies' foreheads remind us of the beauty they hide. A man struck blind can never forget the precious treasure of the sight he has lost. Show me a woman who is extremely beautiful: what use is her beauty except as a note to remind me of the one who surpasses her? Goodbye. You can't teach me to forget.
I'll pay that doctrine, or else die in debt.
I'll teach you that lesson, or die in debt to you.
But Montague is bound as well as I, / In penalty alike; and 'tis not hard, I think, / For men so old as we to keep the peace.
But Montague is bound by the same penalty as I am, and it shouldn't be hard, I think, for men as old as us to keep the peace.
Of honourable reckoning are you both, / And pity 'tis you liv'd at odds so long. / But now my lord, what say you to my suit?
You are both highly respected, and it's a pity you've been enemies for so long. But now, my lord, what do you say to my proposal?

But saying o'er what I have said before. / My child is yet a stranger in the world, / She hath not seen the change of fourteen years; / Let two more summers wither in their pride / Ere we may think her ripe to be a bride.
Only what I've said before. My child is still new to the world: she isn't yet fourteen. Let two more summers fade before we think she's ready to be a bride.
Younger than she are happy mothers made.
Girls younger than her are already happy mothers.

And too soon marr'd are those so early made. / The earth hath swallowed all my hopes but she, / She is the hopeful lady of my earth: / But woo her, gentle Paris, get her heart, / My will to her consent is but a part; / And she agree, within her scope of choice / Lies my consent and fair according voice. / This night I hold an old accustom'd feast, / Whereto I have invited many a guest, / Such as I love, and you among the store, / One more, most welcome, makes my number more. / At my poor house look to behold this night / Earth-treading stars that make dark heaven light: / Such comfort as do lusty young men feel / When well apparell'd April on the heel / Of limping winter treads, even such delight / Among fresh female buds shall you this night / Inherit at my house. Hear all, all see, / And like her most whose merit most shall be: / Which, on more view of many, mine, being one, / May stand in number, though in reckoning none. / Come, go with me. Go, sirrah, trudge about / Through fair Verona; find those persons out / Whose names are written there, [Gives a paper] and to them say, / My house and welcome on their pleasure stay.

And those who marry so young are spoiled too soon. The earth has swallowed all my other children; she is all I have left to hope for and the heir to my lands. But woo her, gentle Paris, win her heart. My wishes are only part of her consent: if she agrees, my approval and willing voice go along with her choice. Tonight I'm holding a traditional feast and have invited many guests I love; you'll be most welcome to add to their number. At my humble house tonight expect to see stars walking on the earth that light up the dark sky. The kind of pleasure lusty young men feel when well-dressed April treads on the heels of limping winter, that delight among fresh young girls will be yours tonight. Listen to them all, look at them all, and like best the one who deserves it most. When you've seen many, my daughter will be one of the number, though she may not count for much. Come with me. Go, boy, hurry through fair Verona and find the people whose names are written here, and tell them my house and my welcome await them.

Find them out whose names are written here! It is written that the / shoemaker should meddle with his yard and the tailor with his last, the / fisher with his pencil, and the painter with his nets; but I am sent to / find those persons whose names are here writ, and can never find what / names the writing person hath here writ. I must to the learned. In good / time!

Find the people whose names are written here! It's written that the shoemaker should busy himself with his tape measure, the tailor with his shoe last, the fisherman with his paintbrush and the painter with his nets. But I've been sent to find the people whose names are written here, and I can't read what names the writer has written. I must find someone educated. And just in time!

Tut, man, one fire burns out another's burning, / One pain is lessen'd by another's anguish; / Turn giddy, and be holp by backward turning; / One desperate grief cures with another's languish: / Take thou some new infection to thy eye, / And the rank poison of the old will die.

Come on, man: one fire burns out another fire's burning, and one pain is eased by another's agony. Spin until you're dizzy and you're cured by spinning the other way. One desperate grief is cured by another's suffering. Let your eye catch a new infection, and the foul poison of the old one will die.
Your plantain leaf is excellent for that.
Your plantain leaf is excellent for that.
Not mad, but bound more than a madman is: / Shut up in prison, kept without my food, / Whipp'd and tormented and—God-den, good fellow.
Not mad, but tied up worse than a madman: locked in prison, starved of food, whipped and tortured, and... Good evening, good fellow.
God gi' go-den. I pray, sir, can you read?
God give you good evening. Please, sir, can you read?
Ay, mine own fortune in my misery.
Yes, I can read my own fortune in my misery.
Perhaps you have learned it without book. / But I pray, can you read anything you see?
Perhaps you learned that by heart, without a book. But please, can you read anything you see?
Ay, If I know the letters and the language.
Yes, if I know the letters and the language.
Ye say honestly, rest you merry!
That's an honest answer. Have a good day!

Signior Martino and his wife and daughters; / County Anselmo and his beauteous sisters; / The lady widow of Utruvio; / Signior Placentio and his lovely nieces; / Mercutio and his brother Valentine; / Mine uncle Capulet, his wife, and daughters; / My fair niece Rosaline and Livia; / Signior Valentio and his cousin Tybalt; / Lucio and the lively Helena.  / A fair assembly. [Gives back the paper] Whither should they come?

'Signior Martino and his wife and daughters; Count Anselmo and his beautiful sisters; the widow of Utruvio; Signior Placentio and his lovely nieces; Mercutio and his brother Valentine; my uncle Capulet, his wife and daughters; my beautiful niece Rosaline, and Livia; Signior Valentio and his cousin Tybalt; Lucio and the lively Helena.' A fine gathering. Where are they meant to come?
Indeed I should have ask'd you that before.
Of course, I should have asked you that first.
Now I'll tell you without asking. My master is the great rich Capulet, / and if you be not of the house of Montagues, I pray come and crush a / cup of wine. Rest you merry.
Now I'll tell you without your asking. My master is the great, rich Capulet, and if you aren't from the Montague household, please come and drink a cup of wine. Have a good day.

At this same ancient feast of Capulet's / Sups the fair Rosaline whom thou so lov'st; / With all the admired beauties of Verona. / Go thither and with unattainted eye, / Compare her face with some that I shall show, / And I will make thee think thy swan a crow.

The beautiful Rosaline, whom you love so much, is having supper at this same traditional feast of Capulet's, with all the most admired beauties of Verona. Go there, and with an unprejudiced eye compare her face with some I'll show you, and I'll make you think your swan is a crow.

When the devout religion of mine eye / Maintains such falsehood, then turn tears to fire; / And these who, often drown'd, could never die, / Transparent heretics, be burnt for liars. / One fairer than my love? The all-seeing sun / Ne'er saw her match since first the world begun.

If my eyes, which worship her like a religion, ever believe such a lie, then let my tears turn to fire, and let these eyes, which have often drowned in tears and never died, be burnt as liars, like see-through heretics. Someone more beautiful than my love? The all-seeing sun has never seen her equal since the world began.

Tut, you saw her fair, none else being by, / Herself pois'd with herself in either eye: / But in that crystal scales let there be weigh'd / Your lady's love against some other maid / That I will show you shining at this feast, / And she shall scant show well that now shows best.

Come on, you saw she was beautiful when no one else was there to compare: she was weighed against herself in each eye. But in those clear scales of your eyes, weigh your lady against some other girl I'll show you shining at this feast, and she'll hardly look good, though she looks best now.
I'll go along, no such sight to be shown, / But to rejoice in splendour of my own.
I'll go along, not to see any such sight, but to enjoy the splendour of my own love.
Nurse, where's my daughter? Call her forth to me.
Nurse, where's my daughter? Call her here to me.
Now, by my maidenhead, at twelve year old, / I bade her come. What, lamb! What ladybird! / God forbid! Where's this girl? What, Juliet!
I swear by my virginity at twelve years old, I told her to come. Come on, lamb! Come on, ladybird! God forbid! Where is that girl? Juliet!
Madam, I am here. What is your will?
Madam, I'm here. What do you want?
This is the matter. Nurse, give leave awhile, / We must talk in secret. Nurse, come back again, / I have remember'd me, thou's hear our counsel. / Thou knowest my daughter's of a pretty age.
This is the matter. Nurse, leave us for a while; we must talk in private. Nurse, come back again: I've remembered, you should hear what we say. You know my daughter is quite grown up now.
Faith, I can tell her age unto an hour.
Indeed, I can tell you her age to the hour.
I'll lay fourteen of my teeth, / And yet, to my teen be it spoken, I have but four, / She is not fourteen. How long is it now / To Lammas-tide?
I'd bet fourteen of my teeth (though, I'm sorry to say, I only have four) that she isn't fourteen. How long is it now to Lammas Day?
Two weeks and a few days.

Even or odd, of all days in the year, / Come Lammas Eve at night shall she be fourteen. / Susan and she,—God rest all Christian souls!— / Were of an age. Well, Susan is with God; / She was too good for me. But as I said, / On Lammas Eve at night shall she be fourteen; / That shall she, marry; I remember it well. / 'Tis since the earthquake now eleven years; / And she was wean'd,—I never shall forget it—, / Of all the days of the year, upon that day: / For I had then laid wormwood to my dug, / Sitting in the sun under the dovehouse wall; / My lord and you were then at Mantua: / Nay, I do bear a brain. But as I said, / When it did taste the wormwood on the nipple / Of my dug and felt it bitter, pretty fool, / To see it tetchy, and fall out with the dug! / Shake, quoth the dovehouse: 'twas no need, I trow, / To bid me trudge. / And since that time it is eleven years; / For then she could stand alone; nay, by th'rood / She could have run and waddled all about; / For even the day before she broke her brow, / And then my husband,—God be with his soul! / A was a merry man,—took up the child: / 'Yea,' quoth he, 'dost thou fall upon thy face? / Thou wilt fall backward when thou hast more wit; / Wilt thou not, Jule?' and, by my holidame, / The pretty wretch left crying, and said 'Ay'. / To see now how a jest shall come about. / I warrant, and I should live a thousand years, / I never should forget it. 'Wilt thou not, Jule?' quoth he; / And, pretty fool, it stinted, and said 'Ay.'

Even or odd, of all the days in the year, she'll be fourteen on the night of Lammas Eve. Susan and she (God rest all Christian souls!) were the same age. Well, Susan is with God: she was too good for me. But as I said, she'll be fourteen on Lammas Eve; yes she will, I remember it well. It's eleven years now since the earthquake, and she was weaned (I'll never forget it) on that very day of all the days of the year. I had put bitter wormwood on my nipple and was sitting in the sun under the dovehouse wall. You and my lord were in Mantua then. Oh, I've a good memory! But as I said, when the pretty little fool tasted the wormwood on my nipple and found it bitter, you should have seen her get cross and fall out with the breast! Then the dovehouse shook with the earthquake, and believe me, nobody needed to tell me to get moving. And it's eleven years since then, because by then she could stand on her own. No, by the cross, she could run and toddle all over the place, because just the day before she'd cut her forehead. And then my husband (God rest his soul, he was a merry man) picked the child up. 'Well,' he said, 'did you fall on your face? You'll fall on your back when you're older, won't you, Jule?' And, by Our Lady, the pretty thing stopped crying and said 'Yes.' Fancy a joke coming true! I swear, if I lived a thousand years I'd never forget it. 'Won't you, Jule?' he said, and the pretty fool stopped and said 'Yes.'
Enough of this; I pray thee hold thy peace.

Yes, madam, yet I cannot choose but laugh, / To think it should leave crying, and say 'Ay'; / And yet I warrant it had upon it brow / A bump as big as a young cockerel's stone; / A perilous knock, and it cried bitterly. / 'Yea,' quoth my husband, 'fall'st upon thy face? / Thou wilt fall backward when thou comest to age; / Wilt thou not, Jule?' it stinted, and said 'Ay'.

Yes, madam. But I can't help laughing to think she stopped crying and said 'Yes'. And yet I swear she had a bump on her forehead as big as a young cockerel's testicle: a dangerous knock, and she cried bitterly. 'Well,' said my husband, 'fall on your face? You'll fall on your back when you're grown up, won't you, Jule?' She stopped and said 'Yes.'
And stint thou too, I pray thee, Nurse, say I.
And you stop too, please, Nurse, I say.
Peace, I have done. God mark thee to his grace / Thou wast the prettiest babe that e'er I nurs'd: / And I might live to see thee married once, I have my wish.
All right, I've finished. God bless you, you were the prettiest baby I ever nursed. If I live to see you married one day, I'll have my wish.
Marry, that marry is the very theme / I came to talk of. Tell me, daughter Juliet, / How stands your disposition to be married?
Well, marriage is exactly what I came to talk about. Tell me, Juliet, my daughter, how do you feel about getting married?
It is an honour that I dream not of.
It's an honour I haven't dreamed of.
An honour! Were not I thine only nurse, / I would say thou hadst suck'd wisdom from thy teat.
An honour! If I weren't the only nurse you had, I'd say you'd sucked wisdom from the breast.

Well, think of marriage now: younger than you, / Here in Verona, ladies of esteem, / Are made already mothers. By my count / I was your mother much upon these years / That you are now a maid. Thus, then, in brief; / The valiant Paris seeks you for his love.

Well, think about marriage now. Here in Verona, ladies of good family younger than you are already mothers. By my count, I was your mother at about the age you are now, still unmarried. So, in brief: the brave Paris wants you as his wife.
A man, young lady! Lady, such a man / As all the world—why he's a man of wax.
What a man, young lady! Lady, such a man as all the world... why, he's as perfect as a wax model.
Verona's summer hath not such a flower.
Verona's summer has no flower like him.
Nay, he's a flower, in faith a very flower.
Yes, he's a flower, honestly, a real flower.

What say you, can you love the gentleman? / This night you shall behold him at our feast; / Read o'er the volume of young Paris' face, / And find delight writ there with beauty's pen. / Examine every married lineament, / And see how one another lends content; / And what obscur'd in this fair volume lies, / Find written in the margent of his eyes. / This precious book of love, this unbound lover, / To beautify him, only lacks a cover: / The fish lives in the sea; and 'tis much pride / For fair without the fair within to hide. / That book in many's eyes doth share the glory, / That in gold clasps locks in the golden story; / So shall you share all that he doth possess, / By having him, making yourself no less.

What do you say? Can you love the gentleman? Tonight you'll see him at our feast. Read the book of young Paris's face and find delight written there by beauty's pen. Study each well-matched feature and see how each one complements the others, and whatever is unclear in this fine book, find it explained in the margin notes of his eyes. This precious book of love, this unbound lover, only needs a cover, a wife, to make him complete. The fish lives in the sea, and it's a fine thing for a beautiful outside to hold a beautiful inside. A book with golden clasps that locks in a golden story is admired by many. In the same way, by having him you'll share everything he owns and lose nothing yourself.
No less, nay bigger. Women grow by men.
Lose nothing? No, grow bigger: women grow bigger through men.
Speak briefly, can you like of Paris' love?
Tell me quickly: can you like Paris's love?
I'll look to like, if looking liking move: / But no more deep will I endart mine eye / Than your consent gives strength to make it fly.
I'll look at him, hoping to like him, if looking can make me like him. But I won't let my eye shoot its dart any deeper than your permission allows.

Madam, the guests are come, supper served up, you called, my young lady / asked for, the Nurse cursed in the pantry, and everything in extremity. / I must hence to wait, I beseech you follow straight.

Madam, the guests have arrived, supper is served, you're being called for, my young lady is being asked for, the Nurse is being cursed in the pantry, and everything is in chaos. I must go and wait on the guests. Please come straight away.
Go, girl, seek happy nights to happy days.
Go, girl, and find happy nights to follow your happy days.
What, shall this speech be spoke for our excuse? / Or shall we on without apology?
Well, shall we make the usual speech to introduce ourselves, or go in without an apology?

The date is out of such prolixity: / We'll have no Cupid hoodwink'd with a scarf, / Bearing a Tartar's painted bow of lath, / Scaring the ladies like a crow-keeper; / Nor no without-book prologue, faintly spoke / After the prompter, for our entrance: / But let them measure us by what they will, / We'll measure them a measure, and be gone.

That kind of long-windedness is out of fashion. We won't have a Cupid blindfolded with a scarf, carrying a painted toy bow made of wood and scaring the ladies like a scarecrow. Nor a prologue spoken feebly after the prompter because we don't know it by heart. Let them judge us however they like: we'll dance them a dance and then go.
Give me a torch, I am not for this ambling; / Being but heavy I will bear the light.
Give me a torch. I'm not in the mood for this prancing about. I'm heavy-hearted, so I'll carry the light.
Nay, gentle Romeo, we must have you dance.
No, gentle Romeo, we must have you dance.
Not I, believe me, you have dancing shoes, / With nimble soles, I have a soul of lead / So stakes me to the ground I cannot move.
Not me, believe me. You have dancing shoes with light soles; I have a soul of lead that pins me to the ground so I can't move.
You are a lover, borrow Cupid's wings, / And soar with them above a common bound.
You're a lover: borrow Cupid's wings and soar above the ordinary leap.
I am too sore enpierced with his shaft / To soar with his light feathers, and so bound, / I cannot bound a pitch above dull woe. / Under love's heavy burden do I sink.
I'm too badly wounded by his arrow to soar on his light feathers, and so tied down that I can't leap an inch above dull misery. I'm sinking under love's heavy weight.
And, to sink in it, should you burden love; / Too great oppression for a tender thing.
And if you sink into it, you'll be a weight on love: too heavy a load for such a tender thing.
Is love a tender thing? It is too rough, / Too rude, too boisterous; and it pricks like thorn.
Is love a tender thing? It's too rough, too rude, too violent, and it pricks like a thorn.

If love be rough with you, be rough with love; / Prick love for pricking, and you beat love down. / Give me a case to put my visage in: [Putting on a mask] / A visor for a visor. What care I / What curious eye doth quote deformities? / Here are the beetle-brows shall blush for me.

If love is rough with you, be rough with love. Prick love back for pricking you, and you'll beat it down. Give me a mask to put my face in. A mask for an ugly face! What do I care if some curious eye notices my ugliness? Here are these bushy eyebrows to blush for me.
Come, knock and enter; and no sooner in / But every man betake him to his legs.
Come on, knock and go in, and as soon as we're inside, every man start dancing.

A torch for me: let wantons, light of heart, / Tickle the senseless rushes with their heels; / For I am proverb'd with a grandsire phrase, / I'll be a candle-holder and look on, / The game was ne'er so fair, and I am done.
A torch for me. Let carefree playboys tickle the floor rushes with their heels. I'll follow the old proverb: I'll hold the candle and watch. The game was never better, and I'm finished.
Tut, dun's the mouse, the constable's own word: / If thou art dun, we'll draw thee from the mire / Or save your reverence love, wherein thou stickest / Up to the ears. Come, we burn daylight, ho.

Nonsense, 'dun's the mouse': keep quiet, as the constable says. If you're Dun the horse, stuck in the mud, we'll pull you out of the mire of this (excuse the word) love you're stuck in up to the ears. Come on, we're burning daylight!
I mean sir, in delay / We waste our lights in vain, light lights by day. / Take our good meaning, for our judgment sits / Five times in that ere once in our five wits.
I mean, sir, by delaying we're wasting our torches, like lighting lamps by day. Take what we mean in good faith: there's five times more sense in that than in our five wits.
And we mean well in going to this mask; / But 'tis no wit to go.
We mean well in going to this masked ball, but it isn't wise to go.
I had a dream last night.
In bed asleep, while they do dream things true.
Lie in bed asleep, while they dream things that are true.

O, then, I see Queen Mab hath been with you. / She is the fairies' midwife, and she comes / In shape no bigger than an agate-stone / On the fore-finger of an alderman, / Drawn with a team of little atomies / Over men's noses as they lie asleep: / Her waggon-spokes made of long spinners' legs; / The cover, of the wings of grasshoppers; / Her traces, of the smallest spider's web; / The collars, of the moonshine's watery beams; / Her whip of cricket's bone; the lash, of film; / Her waggoner, a small grey-coated gnat, / Not half so big as a round little worm / Prick'd from the lazy finger of a maid: / Her chariot is an empty hazelnut, / Made by the joiner squirrel or old grub, / Time out o' mind the fairies' coachmakers. / And in this state she gallops night by night / Through lovers' brains, and then they dream of love; / O'er courtiers' knees, that dream on curtsies straight; / O'er lawyers' fingers, who straight dream on fees; / O'er ladies' lips, who straight on kisses dream, / Which oft the angry Mab with blisters plagues, / Because their breaths with sweetmeats tainted are: / Sometime she gallops o'er a courtier's nose, / And then dreams he of smelling out a suit; / And sometime comes she with a tithe-pig's tail, / Tickling a parson's nose as a lies asleep, / Then dreams he of another benefice: / Sometime she driveth o'er a soldier's neck, / And then dreams he of cutting foreign throats, / Of breaches, ambuscados, Spanish blades, / Of healths five fathom deep; and then anon / Drums in his ear, at which he starts and wakes; / And, being thus frighted, swears a prayer or two, / And sleeps again. This is that very Mab / That plats the manes of horses in the night; / And bakes the elf-locks in foul sluttish hairs, / Which, once untangled, much misfortune bodes: / This is the hag, when maids lie on their backs, / That presses them, and learns them first to bear, / Making them women of good carriage: / This is she,—

Oh, then I see Queen Mab has been with you. She's the fairies' midwife, and she's no bigger than the agate stone in a city councillor's ring. She's drawn by a team of tiny creatures over people's noses as they sleep. Her wagon's spokes are made of spiders' long legs, the cover of grasshoppers' wings, the reins of the finest spider's web, the collars of watery moonbeams. Her whip is a cricket's bone and its lash a thread. Her driver is a small grey-coated gnat, not half as big as the little worm picked out of a lazy girl's finger. Her chariot is an empty hazelnut, made by the squirrel or the old grub, the fairies' coachmakers since time began. In this grand style she gallops night after night through lovers' brains, and then they dream of love; over courtiers' knees, and they dream of bowing; over lawyers' fingers, and they dream of fees; over ladies' lips, and they dream of kisses, though angry Mab often punishes them with blisters because their breath smells of sweets. Sometimes she gallops over a courtier's nose and he dreams of sniffing out a favour to sell. Sometimes she comes with the tail of a pig paid as church tax and tickles a parson's nose as he sleeps, and he dreams of another paid post. Sometimes she drives over a soldier's neck, and he dreams of cutting foreigners' throats, of breaking through walls, ambushes, Spanish swords and huge toasts; then she drums in his ear, and he jumps up and wakes, and being frightened like this, swears a prayer or two and goes back to sleep. This is the same Mab who tangles horses' manes at night and twists dirty hair into elf-knots, which bring bad luck if they're untangled. This is the hag who presses down on girls when they lie on their backs and first teaches them to bear the weight of a man and to carry children. This is she...
Peace, peace, Mercutio, peace, / Thou talk'st of nothing.
Quiet, quiet, Mercutio, quiet! You're talking about nothing.

True, I talk of dreams, / Which are the children of an idle brain, / Begot of nothing but vain fantasy, / Which is as thin of substance as the air, / And more inconstant than the wind, who woos / Even now the frozen bosom of the north, / And, being anger'd, puffs away from thence, / Turning his side to the dew-dropping south.

True, I'm talking about dreams, which are the children of an idle brain, born of nothing but empty fantasy, which is as thin as the air and more changeable than the wind. The wind woos the frozen breast of the north one moment, and then, angry, puffs away from there and turns towards the damp south.
This wind you talk of blows us from ourselves: / Supper is done, and we shall come too late.
This wind you're talking about is blowing us off course. Supper is over, and we'll be too late.

I fear too early: for my mind misgives / Some consequence yet hanging in the stars, / Shall bitterly begin his fearful date / With this night's revels; and expire the term / Of a despised life, clos'd in my breast / By some vile forfeit of untimely death. / But he that hath the steerage of my course / Direct my suit. On, lusty gentlemen!

Too early, I'm afraid. I have a feeling that some event still hanging in the stars will begin its terrible course with tonight's party, and end the term of the hated life inside me with the cruel penalty of an early death. But let whoever steers my course direct my voyage. On, lively gentlemen!
Where's Potpan, that he helps not to take away? / He shift a trencher! He scrape a trencher!
Where's Potpan? Why isn't he helping to clear the table? Him, move a plate! Him, scrape a plate!
When good manners shall lie all in one or two men's hands, and they / unwash'd too, 'tis a foul thing.
When all the good manners are in the hands of one or two men, and their hands unwashed too, it's a bad business.

Away with the join-stools, remove the court-cupboard, look to the / plate. Good thou, save me a piece of marchpane; and as thou loves me, / let the porter let in Susan Grindstone and Nell. Antony and Potpan!
Take away the stools, move the sideboard, look after the silver. Good friend, save me a piece of marzipan, and if you love me, tell the porter to let in Susan Grindstone and Nell. Antony! Potpan!
You are looked for and called for, asked for and sought for, in the / great chamber.
You're being looked for and called for, asked for and searched for, in the great hall.
We cannot be here and there too. Cheerly, boys. Be brisk awhile, and / the longer liver take all.
We can't be here and there at the same time. Cheer up, boys! Be lively for a while, and the one who lives longest takes it all.

Welcome, gentlemen, ladies that have their toes / Unplagu'd with corns will have a bout with you. / Ah my mistresses, which of you all / Will now deny to dance? She that makes dainty, / She I'll swear hath corns. Am I come near ye now? / Welcome, gentlemen! I have seen the day / That I have worn a visor, and could tell / A whispering tale in a fair lady's ear, / Such as would please; 'tis gone, 'tis gone, 'tis gone, / You are welcome, gentlemen! Come, musicians, play. / A hall, a hall, give room! And foot it, girls.

Welcome, gentlemen! Ladies whose toes aren't troubled by corns will have a dance with you. Ah, my ladies, which of you will refuse to dance now? Whoever acts shy, I'll swear she has corns. Have I got you there? Welcome, gentlemen! I remember the days when I wore a mask and could whisper a story in a pretty lady's ear that would please her. Those days are gone, gone, gone. You are welcome, gentlemen! Come, musicians, play. Clear the hall, make room! And dance, girls.

More light, you knaves; and turn the tables up, / And quench the fire, the room is grown too hot. / Ah sirrah, this unlook'd-for sport comes well. / Nay sit, nay sit, good cousin Capulet, / For you and I are past our dancing days; / How long is't now since last yourself and I / Were in a mask?

More light, you rascals, and fold up the tables, and put out the fire: the room has got too hot. Ah, sir, this unexpected fun has turned out well. No, sit down, sit down, good cousin Capulet, because you and I are past our dancing days. How long is it now since you and I last wore masks at a ball?
What, man, 'tis not so much, 'tis not so much: / 'Tis since the nuptial of Lucentio, / Come Pentecost as quickly as it will, / Some five and twenty years; and then we mask'd.
What, man? It's not that long, not that long. It was at Lucentio's wedding. Come Whitsun, whenever it comes, it'll be about twenty-five years. That was when we last wore masks.
'Tis more, 'tis more, his son is elder, sir; / His son is thirty.
It's more, it's more. His son is older than that, sir: his son is thirty.
Will you tell me that? / His son was but a ward two years ago.
Are you telling me that? His son was still a minor two years ago.
What lady is that, which doth enrich the hand / Of yonder knight?
Who is that lady who is honouring the hand of that knight over there?

O, she doth teach the torches to burn bright! / It seems she hangs upon the cheek of night / As a rich jewel in an Ethiop's ear; / Beauty too rich for use, for earth too dear! / So shows a snowy dove trooping with crows / As yonder lady o'er her fellows shows. / The measure done, I'll watch her place of stand, / And touching hers, make blessed my rude hand. / Did my heart love till now? Forswear it, sight! / For I ne'er saw true beauty till this night.

Oh, she teaches the torches how to burn brightly! She seems to hang on the cheek of night like a rich jewel in an African's ear: beauty too rich to be used, too precious for this earth! She stands out among her friends like a snow-white dove in a flock of crows. When this dance is over I'll watch where she stands and bless my rough hand by touching hers. Did my heart ever love until now? Eyes, deny it! I never saw true beauty until tonight.

This by his voice, should be a Montague. / Fetch me my rapier, boy. What, dares the slave / Come hither, cover'd with an antic face, / To fleer and scorn at our solemnity? / Now by the stock and honour of my kin, / To strike him dead I hold it not a sin.

From his voice, this must be a Montague. Fetch me my sword, boy. What? Does the wretch dare come here, his face hidden by a comic mask, to sneer and mock at our celebration? Now, by the ancestry and honour of my family, I don't think it a sin to strike him dead.
Why how now, kinsman! / Wherefore storm you so?
What's the matter, nephew? Why are you raging like this?
Uncle, this is a Montague, our foe; / A villain that is hither come in spite, / To scorn at our solemnity this night.
Uncle, this is a Montague, our enemy, a villain who has come here out of spite to mock our celebration tonight.

Content thee, gentle coz, let him alone, / A bears him like a portly gentleman; / And, to say truth, Verona brags of him / To be a virtuous and well-govern'd youth. / I would not for the wealth of all the town / Here in my house do him disparagement. / Therefore be patient, take no note of him, / It is my will; the which if thou respect, / Show a fair presence and put off these frowns, / An ill-beseeming semblance for a feast.

Calm down, gentle nephew, leave him alone. He behaves like a dignified gentleman, and to tell the truth, Verona boasts of him as a good and well-behaved young man. I wouldn't insult him here in my house for all the wealth in the town. So be patient and ignore him. That's what I want, and if you respect it, put on a pleasant face and stop frowning: that's an unsuitable expression for a feast.
It fits when such a villain is a guest: / I'll not endure him.
It's suitable when such a villain is a guest. I won't put up with him.

He shall be endur'd. / What, goodman boy! I say he shall, go to; / Am I the master here, or you? Go to. / You'll not endure him! God shall mend my soul, / You'll make a mutiny among my guests! / You will set cock-a-hoop, you'll be the man!

He will be put up with. What, boy! I say he will. Go on! Am I the master here, or you? Go on! You won't put up with him! God save my soul, you'd start a riot among my guests! You'd throw everything into chaos! You'd play the big man!

Go to, go to! / You are a saucy boy. Is't so, indeed? / This trick may chance to scathe you, I know what. / You must contrary me! Marry, 'tis time. / Well said, my hearts!—You are a princox; go: / Be quiet, or—More light, more light!—For shame! / I'll make you quiet. What, cheerly, my hearts.

Go on, go on! You're an insolent boy. Is that so? This behaviour may come back to hurt you, I know what I'm talking about. You have to contradict me! Well, it's about time... Well done, my friends! You're a cheeky young pup. Go! Be quiet, or... More light, more light! For shame! I'll make you be quiet. Cheer up, my friends!
Patience perforce with wilful choler meeting / Makes my flesh tremble in their different greeting. / I will withdraw: but this intrusion shall, / Now seeming sweet, convert to bitter gall.
Forced patience meeting with deliberate anger makes my body shake at the clash between them. I'll go, but this intrusion, which seems sweet now, will turn into bitter poison.
[To Juliet] If I profane with my unworthiest hand / This holy shrine, the gentle sin is this, / My lips, two blushing pilgrims, ready stand / To smooth that rough touch with a tender kiss.

If I make this holy shrine, your hand, unholy by touching it with my unworthy hand, this is the gentle penance: my lips, two blushing pilgrims, are ready to smooth away that rough touch with a tender kiss.
Good pilgrim, you do wrong your hand too much, / Which mannerly devotion shows in this; / For saints have hands that pilgrims' hands do touch, / And palm to palm is holy palmers' kiss.
Good pilgrim, you're too hard on your hand, which shows proper devotion in this. Saints have hands that pilgrims' hands may touch, and palm to palm is the holy pilgrims' kiss.
Have not saints lips, and holy palmers too?
Don't saints have lips, and holy pilgrims too?
Ay, pilgrim, lips that they must use in prayer.
Yes, pilgrim: lips that they must use for prayer.
O, then, dear saint, let lips do what hands do: / They pray, grant thou, lest faith turn to despair.
Oh, then, dear saint, let lips do what hands do. They pray: grant their prayer, or faith will turn to despair.
Saints do not move, though grant for prayers' sake.
Saints don't move, though they grant prayers.
Then move not while my prayer's effect I take. / Thus from my lips, by thine my sin is purg'd.
Then don't move while I receive what I prayed for. So, by your lips, my sin is washed from mine.
Then have my lips the sin that they have took.
Then my lips have the sin they took from yours.
Sin from my lips? O trespass sweetly urg'd! / Give me my sin again.
Sin from my lips? Oh, a crime so sweetly urged! Give me my sin back.
Madam, your mother craves a word with you.
Madam, your mother wants a word with you.

Marry, bachelor, / Her mother is the lady of the house, / And a good lady, and a wise and virtuous. / I nurs'd her daughter that you talk'd withal. / I tell you, he that can lay hold of her / Shall have the chinks.
Why, young man, her mother is the lady of the house, and a good lady, and wise and virtuous. I nursed her daughter, the one you were talking to. I tell you, whoever gets hold of her will be rich.
Is she a Capulet? / O dear account! My life is my foe's debt.
Is she a Capulet? Oh, a costly bargain! My life is in my enemy's debt.
Away, be gone; the sport is at the best.
Let's go: the fun is at its best.
Ay, so I fear; the more is my unrest.
Yes, I'm afraid so. That makes me all the more uneasy.

Nay, gentlemen, prepare not to be gone, / We have a trifling foolish banquet towards. / Is it e'en so? Why then, I thank you all; / I thank you, honest gentlemen; good night. / More torches here! Come on then, let's to bed. / Ah, sirrah, by my fay, it waxes late, / I'll to my rest.

No, gentlemen, don't get ready to go: we have a small, simple dessert coming. Is that how it is? Well then, I thank you all. Thank you, good gentlemen. Good night. More torches here! Come on then, let's go to bed. Ah, sir, by my faith, it's getting late. I'm going to bed.
Come hither, Nurse. What is yond gentleman?
Come here, Nurse. Who is that gentleman?
The son and heir of old Tiberio.
The son and heir of old Tiberio.
What's he that now is going out of door?
Who is that going out of the door now?
Marry, that I think be young Petruchio.
Well, I think that's young Petruchio.
What's he that follows here, that would not dance?
Who's that following him, the one who wouldn't dance?
Go ask his name. If he be married, / My grave is like to be my wedding bed.
Go and ask his name. If he's married, my grave is likely to be my wedding bed.
His name is Romeo, and a Montague, / The only son of your great enemy.
His name is Romeo, and he's a Montague, the only son of your great enemy.
My only love sprung from my only hate! / Too early seen unknown, and known too late! / Prodigious birth of love it is to me, / That I must love a loathed enemy.
My only love born from my only hate! I saw him too early without knowing who he was, and I know too late! This birth of love is a monstrous omen for me, that I must love a hated enemy.
A rhyme I learn'd even now / Of one I danc'd withal.
A rhyme I learned just now from someone I danced with.
Anon, anon! / Come let's away, the strangers all are gone.
Coming, coming! Come on, let's go. The guests have all gone.

Now old desire doth in his deathbed lie, / And young affection gapes to be his heir; / That fair for which love groan'd for and would die, / With tender Juliet match'd, is now not fair. / Now Romeo is belov'd, and loves again, / Alike bewitched by the charm of looks; / But to his foe suppos'd he must complain, / And she steal love's sweet bait from fearful hooks: / Being held a foe, he may not have access / To breathe such vows as lovers use to swear; / And she as much in love, her means much less / To meet her new beloved anywhere. / But passion lends them power, time means, to meet, / Tempering extremities with extreme sweet.

Now Romeo's old desire for Rosaline lies on its deathbed, and a young love is eager to inherit its place. The beauty he groaned for and would have died for no longer seems beautiful compared with tender Juliet. Now Romeo is loved and loves in return, both of them bewitched by each other's looks. But he must plead his love to someone he thinks is his enemy, and she must steal love's sweet bait from dangerous hooks. Because he is thought of as an enemy, he can't get near her to speak the vows lovers usually swear, and she, just as much in love, has even less chance of meeting her new love anywhere. But passion gives them the strength, and time gives them the chance, to meet, softening their great dangers with great sweetness.
Can I go forward when my heart is here? / Turn back, dull earth, and find thy centre out.
How can I go on when my heart is here? Turn back, dull body, and find your centre, your heart.
He is wise, / And on my life hath stol'n him home to bed.
He's sensible. I bet my life he's slipped off home to bed.
He ran this way, and leap'd this orchard wall: / Call, good Mercutio.
He ran this way and jumped over this orchard wall. Call him, good Mercutio.

Nay, I'll conjure too. / Romeo! Humours! Madman! Passion! Lover! / Appear thou in the likeness of a sigh, / Speak but one rhyme, and I am satisfied; / Cry but 'Ah me!' Pronounce but Love and dove; / Speak to my gossip Venus one fair word, / One nickname for her purblind son and heir, / Young Abraham Cupid, he that shot so trim / When King Cophetua lov'd the beggar-maid. / He heareth not, he stirreth not, he moveth not; / The ape is dead, and I must conjure him. / I conjure thee by Rosaline's bright eyes, / By her high forehead and her scarlet lip, / By her fine foot, straight leg, and quivering thigh, / And the demesnes that there adjacent lie, / That in thy likeness thou appear to us.

No, I'll summon him with spells too. Romeo! Moods! Madman! Passion! Lover! Appear in the shape of a sigh. Speak just one rhyme and I'll be satisfied. Just cry 'Ah me!' Just say 'love' and 'dove'. Say one nice word to my friend Venus, and give one nickname to her half-blind son and heir, young Cupid, who shot so accurately when King Cophetua fell in love with the beggar girl. He doesn't hear, he doesn't stir, he doesn't move. The monkey is playing dead, so I must summon him with spells. I summon you by Rosaline's bright eyes, by her high forehead and her red lip, by her fine foot, straight leg and quivering thigh, and the regions lying next to it, to appear to us in your own shape.
An if he hear thee, thou wilt anger him.
If he hears you, you'll make him angry.

This cannot anger him. 'Twould anger him / To raise a spirit in his mistress' circle, / Of some strange nature, letting it there stand / Till she had laid it, and conjur'd it down; / That were some spite. My invocation / Is fair and honest, and, in his mistress' name, / I conjure only but to raise up him.

This can't make him angry. It would make him angry if I raised some strange spirit in his mistress's magic circle and left it standing there until she had made it go down. That would be spiteful. My spell is fair and honest: I'm only using his mistress's name to raise him up.
Come, he hath hid himself among these trees / To be consorted with the humorous night. / Blind is his love, and best befits the dark.
Come on, he's hidden himself among these trees to keep company with the moody night. His love is blind and suits the dark best.

If love be blind, love cannot hit the mark. / Now will he sit under a medlar tree, / And wish his mistress were that kind of fruit / As maids call medlars when they laugh alone. / O Romeo, that she were, O that she were / An open-arse and thou a poperin pear! / Romeo, good night. I'll to my truckle-bed. / This field-bed is too cold for me to sleep. / Come, shall we go?

If love is blind, love can't hit the target. Now he'll sit under a medlar tree and wish his mistress were the kind of fruit girls joke about when they laugh alone. Oh Romeo, if only she were an open-arse and you a poperin pear! Romeo, good night. I'm off to my little bed: this open-air bed is too cold for me to sleep in. Come on, shall we go?
Go then; for 'tis in vain / To seek him here that means not to be found.
Let's go, then. It's pointless looking here for someone who doesn't want to be found.
He jests at scars that never felt a wound.
He makes fun of scars who has never been wounded.

But soft, what light through yonder window breaks? / It is the east, and Juliet is the sun! / Arise fair sun and kill the envious moon, / Who is already sick and pale with grief, / That thou her maid art far more fair than she. / Be not her maid since she is envious; / Her vestal livery is but sick and green, / And none but fools do wear it; cast it off. / It is my lady, O it is my love! / O, that she knew she were! / She speaks, yet she says nothing. What of that? / Her eye discourses, I will answer it. / I am too bold, 'tis not to me she speaks. / Two of the fairest stars in all the heaven, / Having some business, do entreat her eyes / To twinkle in their spheres till they return. / What if her eyes were there, they in her head? / The brightness of her cheek would shame those stars, / As daylight doth a lamp; her eyes in heaven / Would through the airy region stream so bright / That birds would sing and think it were not night. / See how she leans her cheek upon her hand. / O that I were a glove upon that hand, / That I might touch that cheek.

But wait, what light is that breaking through the window up there? It is the east, and Juliet is the sun! Rise, beautiful sun, and kill the jealous moon, who is already sick and pale with grief because you, her servant, are far more beautiful than she is. Don't serve her, since she is jealous. Her virgin's uniform is sickly green, and only fools wear it: throw it off. It's my lady, oh, it's my love! Oh, if only she knew she was! She speaks, but says nothing. What does that matter? Her eyes are speaking; I'll answer them. I'm too bold: she isn't speaking to me. Two of the most beautiful stars in all the sky have business elsewhere and are asking her eyes to shine in their places until they return. What if her eyes were up there, and the stars in her head? The brightness of her cheek would shame those stars as daylight shames a lamp. Her eyes in the sky would shine so brightly through the air that birds would sing and think it wasn't night. Look how she leans her cheek on her hand. Oh, if only I were a glove on that hand, so that I could touch that cheek!

She speaks. / O speak again bright angel, for thou art / As glorious to this night, being o'er my head, / As is a winged messenger of heaven / Unto the white-upturned wondering eyes / Of mortals that fall back to gaze on him / When he bestrides the lazy-puffing clouds / And sails upon the bosom of the air.

She speaks. Oh, speak again, bright angel! Up there above my head, you are as glorious to this night as a winged messenger from heaven is to the wondering eyes of human beings, who bend back and look up, their eyes showing their whites, to gaze at him as he rides the lazily drifting clouds and sails on the breast of the air.
O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo? / Deny thy father and refuse thy name. / Or if thou wilt not, be but sworn my love, / And I'll no longer be a Capulet.
Oh Romeo, Romeo, why are you Romeo? Reject your father and refuse your name. Or if you won't, just swear you love me, and I'll stop being a Capulet.
[Aside] Shall I hear more, or shall I speak at this?
Shall I listen to more, or shall I speak now?

'Tis but thy name that is my enemy; / Thou art thyself, though not a Montague. / What's Montague? It is nor hand nor foot, / Nor arm, nor face, nor any other part / Belonging to a man. O be some other name. / What's in a name? That which we call a rose / By any other name would smell as sweet; / So Romeo would, were he not Romeo call'd, / Retain that dear perfection which he owes / Without that title. Romeo, doff thy name, / And for thy name, which is no part of thee, / Take all myself.

It's only your name that is my enemy. You'd still be yourself even if you weren't a Montague. What is a Montague? It isn't a hand or a foot, or an arm, or a face, or any other part of a man. Oh, be some other name! What's in a name? The thing we call a rose would smell just as sweet if we called it anything else. In the same way Romeo, if he weren't called Romeo, would keep the dear perfection he has without that title. Romeo, throw off your name, and in exchange for your name, which isn't part of you, take all of me.
I take thee at thy word. / Call me but love, and I'll be new baptis'd; / Henceforth I never will be Romeo.
I'll take you at your word. Just call me 'love', and I'll be baptised again with a new name. From now on I'll never be Romeo.
What man art thou that, thus bescreen'd in night / So stumblest on my counsel?
Who are you, hidden by the dark like this, stumbling on my private thoughts?
By a name / I know not how to tell thee who I am: / My name, dear saint, is hateful to myself, / Because it is an enemy to thee. / Had I it written, I would tear the word.
I don't know how to tell you who I am by giving a name. My name, dear saint, is hateful to me, because it is your enemy. If I had it written down, I'd tear up the word.
My ears have yet not drunk a hundred words / Of thy tongue's utterance, yet I know the sound. / Art thou not Romeo, and a Montague?
My ears haven't yet drunk in a hundred words from your mouth, but I know the sound. Aren't you Romeo, and a Montague?
Neither, fair maid, if either thee dislike.
Neither, beautiful girl, if you dislike either.
How cam'st thou hither, tell me, and wherefore? / The orchard walls are high and hard to climb, / And the place death, considering who thou art, / If any of my kinsmen find thee here.
How did you get here, tell me, and why? The orchard walls are high and hard to climb, and this place means death, considering who you are, if any of my relatives find you here.
With love's light wings did I o'erperch these walls, / For stony limits cannot hold love out, / And what love can do, that dares love attempt: / Therefore thy kinsmen are no stop to me.
I flew over these walls on love's light wings, because stone barriers can't keep love out, and whatever love can do, love dares to try. So your relatives can't stop me.
If they do see thee, they will murder thee.
If they see you, they'll murder you.
Alack, there lies more peril in thine eye / Than twenty of their swords. Look thou but sweet, / And I am proof against their enmity.
Oh, there's more danger in your eyes than in twenty of their swords. Just look sweetly at me, and I'm protected against their hatred.
I would not for the world they saw thee here.
I wouldn't have them see you here for all the world.
I have night's cloak to hide me from their eyes, / And but thou love me, let them find me here. / My life were better ended by their hate / Than death prorogued, wanting of thy love.

I have the night's cloak to hide me from their eyes. And unless you love me, let them find me here: it would be better for my life to end by their hatred than for death to be delayed while I lack your love.
By whose direction found'st thou out this place?
Who told you how to find this place?

By love, that first did prompt me to enquire; / He lent me counsel, and I lent him eyes. / I am no pilot; yet wert thou as far / As that vast shore wash'd with the farthest sea, / I should adventure for such merchandise.

Love, who first urged me to look for it. He gave me advice, and I gave him eyes. I'm no sailor, but if you were as far away as the vast shore washed by the farthest sea, I'd risk the voyage for such a treasure.

Thou knowest the mask of night is on my face, / Else would a maiden blush bepaint my cheek / For that which thou hast heard me speak tonight. / Fain would I dwell on form, fain, fain deny / What I have spoke; but farewell compliment. / Dost thou love me? I know thou wilt say Ay, / And I will take thy word. Yet, if thou swear'st, / Thou mayst prove false. At lovers' perjuries, / They say Jove laughs. O gentle Romeo, / If thou dost love, pronounce it faithfully. / Or if thou thinkest I am too quickly won, / I'll frown and be perverse, and say thee nay, / So thou wilt woo. But else, not for the world. / In truth, fair Montague, I am too fond; / And therefore thou mayst think my 'haviour light: / But trust me, gentleman, I'll prove more true / Than those that have more cunning to be strange. / I should have been more strange, I must confess, / But that thou overheard'st, ere I was 'ware, / My true-love passion; therefore pardon me, / And not impute this yielding to light love, / Which the dark night hath so discovered.

You know the darkness of night masks my face, or else you'd see me blush like a girl for what you've heard me say tonight. I'd gladly keep to the proper formalities, gladly, gladly deny what I've said. But goodbye to good manners! Do you love me? I know you'll say 'Yes', and I'll take your word. But if you swear it, you may turn out to be false: they say Jove laughs at lovers' broken promises. Oh gentle Romeo, if you do love me, say so sincerely. Or if you think I'm won too quickly, I'll frown and be difficult and say no to you, so that you'll woo me. But otherwise, not for the world. Honestly, handsome Montague, I'm too much in love, and so you may think my behaviour is loose. But trust me, gentleman, I'll prove more faithful than girls who are more skilled at playing hard to get. I should have been more reserved, I admit, except that you overheard my true love's passion before I knew you were there. So forgive me, and don't think my giving in like this is cheap love, which the dark night has revealed.
Lady, by yonder blessed moon I vow, / That tips with silver all these fruit-tree tops,—
Lady, I swear by that blessed moon up there, which tips all these fruit trees with silver...
O swear not by the moon, th'inconstant moon, / That monthly changes in her circled orb, / Lest that thy love prove likewise variable.
Oh, don't swear by the moon, the changeable moon that alters every month in its circling orbit, in case your love turns out just as changeable.
Do not swear at all. / Or if thou wilt, swear by thy gracious self, / Which is the god of my idolatry, / And I'll believe thee.
Don't swear at all. Or if you must, swear by your gracious self, which is the god I worship, and I'll believe you.

Well, do not swear. Although I joy in thee, / I have no joy of this contract tonight; / It is too rash, too unadvis'd, too sudden, / Too like the lightning, which doth cease to be / Ere one can say "It lightens." Sweet, good night. / This bud of love, by summer's ripening breath, / May prove a beauteous flower when next we meet. / Good night, good night. As sweet repose and rest / Come to thy heart as that within my breast.

Well, don't swear. Although you are my joy, I take no joy in this agreement tonight. It's too rash, too unconsidered, too sudden, too like the lightning, which stops existing before you can say 'It's lightning.' Sweet, good night. This bud of love, ripened by the breath of summer, may turn into a beautiful flower when we next meet. Good night, good night. May the same sweet peace and rest come to your heart as is in mine.
O wilt thou leave me so unsatisfied?
Oh, will you leave me so unsatisfied?
What satisfaction canst thou have tonight?
What satisfaction can you have tonight?
Th'exchange of thy love's faithful vow for mine.
The exchange of your faithful vow of love for mine.
I gave thee mine before thou didst request it; / And yet I would it were to give again.
I gave you mine before you asked for it, and yet I wish I had it to give again.
Would'st thou withdraw it? For what purpose, love?
Would you take it back? Why, my love?

But to be frank and give it thee again. / And yet I wish but for the thing I have; / My bounty is as boundless as the sea, / My love as deep; the more I give to thee, / The more I have, for both are infinite. / I hear some noise within. Dear love, adieu.

Only to be generous and give it to you again. And yet I'm wishing for something I already have. My generosity is as limitless as the sea, and my love as deep: the more I give to you, the more I have, because both are infinite. I hear a noise inside. Dear love, goodbye.
Anon, good Nurse!—Sweet Montague be true. / Stay but a little, I will come again.
Coming, good Nurse! Sweet Montague, be true. Wait just a little; I'll come back.
O blessed, blessed night. I am afeard, / Being in night, all this is but a dream, / Too flattering sweet to be substantial.
Oh blessed, blessed night! I'm afraid, because it's night, that all this is only a dream, too pleasing and sweet to be real.

Three words, dear Romeo, and good night indeed. / If that thy bent of love be honourable, / Thy purpose marriage, send me word tomorrow, / By one that I'll procure to come to thee, / Where and what time thou wilt perform the rite, / And all my fortunes at thy foot I'll lay / And follow thee my lord throughout the world.

Three words, dear Romeo, and then good night for real. If your love is honourable and you intend marriage, send me word tomorrow, by someone I'll arrange to send to you, of where and when you'll perform the ceremony, and I'll lay all my fortunes at your feet and follow you, my lord, throughout the world.
I come, anon.— But if thou meanest not well, / I do beseech thee,—
I'm coming, in a moment! But if you don't mean well, I beg you...
By and by I come— / To cease thy strife and leave me to my grief. / Tomorrow will I send.
I'm coming right away! ...to stop your courtship and leave me to my grief. I'll send someone tomorrow.
As my soul hopes to be saved...
A thousand times the worse, to want thy light. / Love goes toward love as schoolboys from their books, / But love from love, towards school with heavy looks.
It's a thousand times worse without your light. Love goes towards love like schoolboys running away from their books, but love leaves love like schoolboys heading to school with gloomy faces.

Hist! Romeo, hist! O for a falconer's voice / To lure this tassel-gentle back again. / Bondage is hoarse and may not speak aloud, / Else would I tear the cave where Echo lies, / And make her airy tongue more hoarse than mine / With repetition of my Romeo's name.

Psst! Romeo, psst! Oh, for a falconer's call, to lure this fine male falcon back again! Being kept in, I have to whisper and can't speak out loud, or else I'd tear open the cave where Echo lives and make her airy voice hoarser than mine by repeating my Romeo's name.
It is my soul that calls upon my name. / How silver-sweet sound lovers' tongues by night, / Like softest music to attending ears.
It's my soul that's calling my name. How silver-sweet lovers' voices sound at night, like the softest music to listening ears!
What o'clock tomorrow / Shall I send to thee?
At what time tomorrow shall I send to you?
I will not fail. 'Tis twenty years till then. / I have forgot why I did call thee back.
I won't fail. It's twenty years till then. I've forgotten why I called you back.
Let me stand here till thou remember it.
Let me stand here till you remember it.
I shall forget, to have thee still stand there, / Remembering how I love thy company.
I'll keep forgetting, so that you'll keep standing there, remembering only how much I love your company.
And I'll still stay, to have thee still forget, / Forgetting any other home but this.
And I'll keep staying, so that you keep forgetting, and I'll forget any home but this.
