'Tis almost morning; I would have thee gone, / And yet no farther than a wanton's bird, / That lets it hop a little from her hand, / Like a poor prisoner in his twisted gyves, / And with a silk thread plucks it back again, / So loving-jealous of his liberty.

It's almost morning. I want you to go, but no further than a spoilt child's pet bird, which she lets hop a little way from her hand, like a poor prisoner in tangled chains, and then pulls back with a silk thread, so lovingly jealous of its freedom.
I would I were thy bird.
I wish I were your bird.
Sweet, so would I: / Yet I should kill thee with much cherishing. / Good night, good night. Parting is such sweet sorrow / That I shall say good night till it be morrow.
Sweet, so do I. But I'd kill you with too much loving. Good night, good night. Parting is such sweet sorrow that I'll keep saying good night until it's morning.
Sleep dwell upon thine eyes, peace in thy breast. / Would I were sleep and peace, so sweet to rest. / Hence will I to my ghostly Sire's cell, / His help to crave and my dear hap to tell.

May sleep rest on your eyes, and peace in your heart. I wish I were sleep and peace, to rest in such a sweet place. From here I'll go to my holy father's cell, to ask for his help and tell him my good luck.

The grey-ey'd morn smiles on the frowning night, / Chequering the eastern clouds with streaks of light; / And fleckled darkness like a drunkard reels / From forth day's pathway, made by Titan's fiery wheels / Now, ere the sun advance his burning eye, / The day to cheer, and night's dank dew to dry, / I must upfill this osier cage of ours / With baleful weeds and precious-juiced flowers. / The earth that's nature's mother, is her tomb; / What is her burying grave, that is her womb: / And from her womb children of divers kind / We sucking on her natural bosom find. / Many for many virtues excellent, / None but for some, and yet all different. / O, mickle is the powerful grace that lies / In plants, herbs, stones, and their true qualities. / For naught so vile that on the earth doth live / But to the earth some special good doth give; / Nor aught so good but, strain'd from that fair use, / Revolts from true birth, stumbling on abuse. / Virtue itself turns vice being misapplied, / And vice sometime's by action dignified.

The grey-eyed morning smiles on the frowning night, marking the eastern clouds with streaks of light, and the spotted darkness staggers like a drunkard out of the path of day and the sun god's fiery wheels. Now, before the sun lifts its burning eye to cheer the day and dry the night's damp dew, I must fill this willow basket of mine with poisonous weeds and flowers with precious juices. The earth, which is nature's mother, is also her tomb. What is her grave is also her womb, and from her womb we find children of many kinds feeding at her breast. Many have many excellent qualities; none is without some, and yet all are different. Oh, there is great power for good in plants, herbs and stones, and their true properties. Nothing that lives on earth is so evil that it doesn't do the earth some special good, and nothing is so good that, if it's forced away from its proper use, it doesn't rebel against its true nature and fall into misuse. Virtue itself turns into vice if it's misapplied, and vice is sometimes made worthy by the right action.

Within the infant rind of this weak flower / Poison hath residence, and medicine power: / For this, being smelt, with that part cheers each part; / Being tasted, slays all senses with the heart. / Two such opposed kings encamp them still / In man as well as herbs,—grace and rude will; / And where the worser is predominant, / Full soon the canker death eats up that plant.

Inside the tender skin of this little flower live both poison and medicine. Smelt, this part cheers every part of the body; tasted, it kills all the senses along with the heart. Two such opposing kings are always camped in men as well as in plants: goodness and coarse desire. And where the worse one rules, the cankerworm of death soon eats up that plant.

Benedicite! / What early tongue so sweet saluteth me? / Young son, it argues a distemper'd head / So soon to bid good morrow to thy bed. / Care keeps his watch in every old man's eye, / And where care lodges sleep will never lie; / But where unbruised youth with unstuff'd brain / Doth couch his limbs, there golden sleep doth reign. / Therefore thy earliness doth me assure / Thou art uprous'd with some distemperature; / Or if not so, then here I hit it right, / Our Romeo hath not been in bed tonight.

Bless you! Whose early voice is greeting me so sweetly? Young son, it suggests a troubled mind to be saying good morning to your bed so soon. Worry keeps watch in every old man's eye, and where worry lives, sleep will never stay. But where untroubled youth with an uncluttered brain lies down to rest, golden sleep rules. So your early rising tells me you've been woken by some disturbance. Or if not, then I've got it right this time: our Romeo hasn't been to bed tonight.
That last is true; the sweeter rest was mine.
That last part is true. The rest I had was sweeter than sleep.
God pardon sin. Wast thou with Rosaline?
God forgive sin! Were you with Rosaline?
With Rosaline, my ghostly father? No. / I have forgot that name, and that name's woe.
With Rosaline, my holy father? No. I've forgotten that name and the misery it brought.
That's my good son. But where hast thou been then?
That's my good son. But where have you been, then?

I'll tell thee ere thou ask it me again. / I have been feasting with mine enemy, / Where on a sudden one hath wounded me / That's by me wounded. Both our remedies / Within thy help and holy physic lies. / I bear no hatred, blessed man; for lo, / My intercession likewise steads my foe.

I'll tell you before you need to ask again. I've been feasting with my enemy, where suddenly someone wounded me whom I've also wounded. The cure for both of us lies in your help and holy medicine. I bear no hatred, blessed man, because look: my request helps my enemy as well.
Be plain, good son, and homely in thy drift; / Riddling confession finds but riddling shrift.
Speak plainly, good son, and simply. A riddling confession only gets a riddling forgiveness.

Then plainly know my heart's dear love is set / On the fair daughter of rich Capulet. / As mine on hers, so hers is set on mine; / And all combin'd, save what thou must combine / By holy marriage. When, and where, and how / We met, we woo'd, and made exchange of vow, / I'll tell thee as we pass; but this I pray, / That thou consent to marry us today.

Then let me tell you plainly: my heart's dear love is set on the beautiful daughter of rich Capulet. As mine is set on her, hers is set on me, and everything is agreed, except what you must join by holy marriage. When, where and how we met, wooed and exchanged vows, I'll tell you as we walk. But this I beg: that you agree to marry us today.

Holy Saint Francis! What a change is here! / Is Rosaline, that thou didst love so dear, / So soon forsaken? Young men's love then lies / Not truly in their hearts, but in their eyes. / Jesu Maria, what a deal of brine / Hath wash'd thy sallow cheeks for Rosaline! / How much salt water thrown away in waste, / To season love, that of it doth not taste. / The sun not yet thy sighs from heaven clears, / Thy old groans yet ring in mine ancient ears. / Lo here upon thy cheek the stain doth sit / Of an old tear that is not wash'd off yet. / If ere thou wast thyself, and these woes thine, / Thou and these woes were all for Rosaline, / And art thou chang'd? Pronounce this sentence then, / Women may fall, when there's no strength in men.

Holy Saint Francis, what a change this is! Is Rosaline, whom you loved so dearly, abandoned so quickly? Then young men's love doesn't really lie in their hearts, but in their eyes. Jesus and Mary, what a lot of salt water washed your pale cheeks for Rosaline! How much salt water was thrown away and wasted to flavour a love that you've now lost the taste for! The sun hasn't yet cleared your sighs from the sky; your old groans are still ringing in my old ears. Look, here on your cheek is the stain of an old tear that hasn't been washed off yet. If you were ever yourself, and these griefs were yours, you and your griefs were all for Rosaline. And have you changed? Then repeat this saying after me: women may fall when men have no strength.
Thou chidd'st me oft for loving Rosaline.
You often told me off for loving Rosaline.
For doting, not for loving, pupil mine.
For being infatuated, not for loving, my pupil.
And told me to bury my love.
Not in a grave / To lay one in, another out to have.
Not in a grave, so that you could put one love in it and take another out.
I pray thee chide me not, her I love now / Doth grace for grace and love for love allow. / The other did not so.
Please don't scold me. The one I love now returns favour for favour and love for love. The other one didn't.

O, she knew well / Thy love did read by rote, that could not spell. / But come young waverer, come go with me, / In one respect I'll thy assistant be; / For this alliance may so happy prove, / To turn your households' rancour to pure love.

Oh, she knew well that your love was reciting words it had learned by heart without being able to spell. But come, young waverer, come with me. For one reason I'll help you: this marriage may turn out so well that it changes your families' hatred into pure love.
O let us hence; I stand on sudden haste.
Oh, let's go! I need to hurry.
Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast.
Wisely and slowly. Those who run fast stumble.
Where the devil should this Romeo be? Came he not home tonight?
Where the devil can this Romeo be? Didn't he come home last night?
Not to his father's; I spoke with his man.
Not to his father's. I spoke to his servant.
Why, that same pale hard-hearted wench, that Rosaline, torments him so / that he will sure run mad.
Why, that same pale, hard-hearted girl, that Rosaline, torments him so much that he'll certainly go mad.
Tybalt, the kinsman to old Capulet, hath sent a letter to his father's / house.
Tybalt, old Capulet's nephew, has sent a letter to Romeo's father's house.
A challenge to a duel, I'd bet my life.
Any man that can write may answer a letter.
Any man who can write can answer a letter.
Nay, he will answer the letter's master, how he dares, being dared.
No, he'll answer the man who wrote it: show how he dares when he's dared.

Alas poor Romeo, he is already dead, stabbed with a white wench's black / eye; run through the ear with a love song, the very pin of his heart / cleft with the blind bow-boy's butt-shaft. And is he a man to encounter / Tybalt?

Oh, poor Romeo, he's already dead! Stabbed by a pale girl's dark eye, shot through the ear with a love song, the very centre of his heart split by blind Cupid's practice arrow. And is he the man to take on Tybalt?
Why, what's so special about Tybalt?

More than Prince of cats. O, he's the courageous captain of / compliments. He fights as you sing prick-song, keeps time, distance, / and proportion. He rests his minim rest, one, two, and the third in / your bosom: the very butcher of a silk button, a duellist, a duellist; / a gentleman of the very first house, of the first and second cause. Ah, / the immortal passado, the punto reverso, the hay.

He's more than the Prince of Cats, I can tell you. Oh, he's the brave master of the fencing rules. He fights the way you sing from sheet music: he keeps time, distance and rhythm. He pauses for the shortest rest, one, two, and the third is in your chest. He's a real butcher of silk buttons, a duellist, a duellist, a gentleman of the very best fencing school, who knows every rule of when to fight. Ah, the immortal passado! The punto reverso! The hai!

The pox of such antic lisping, affecting phantasies; these new tuners / of accent. By Jesu, a very good blade, a very tall man, a very good / whore. Why, is not this a lamentable thing, grandsire, that we should / be thus afflicted with these strange flies, these fashion-mongers, / these pardon-me's, who stand so much on the new form that they cannot / sit at ease on the old bench? O their bones, their bones!

A plague on these ridiculous, lisping, affected show-offs, these new-fangled talkers! 'By Jesus, a very good blade! A very brave man! A very good whore!' Isn't it a sad thing, old man, that we should be pestered by these foreign flies, these fashion-mongers, these 'pardon-me's, who care so much about new manners that they can't sit comfortably on the old bench? Oh, their 'bon's, their 'bon's!
Here comes Romeo, here comes Romeo!
Here comes Romeo, here comes Romeo!

Without his roe, like a dried herring. O flesh, flesh, how art thou / fishified! Now is he for the numbers that Petrarch flowed in. Laura, to / his lady, was but a kitchen wench,—marry, she had a better love to / berhyme her: Dido a dowdy; Cleopatra a gypsy; Helen and Hero hildings / and harlots; Thisbe a grey eye or so, but not to the purpose. Signior / Romeo, bonjour! There's a French salutation to your French slop. You / gave us the counterfeit fairly last night.

Without his roe, like a dried herring: only half of himself. Oh flesh, flesh, how you've been turned into fish! Now he's ready for the kind of verse Petrarch poured out. Compared with his lady, Laura was just a kitchen maid (though she had a better lover to write rhymes about her); Dido was a frump, Cleopatra a gypsy, Helen and Hero worthless whores, and Thisbe had a pretty eye or so, but nothing to speak of. Signior Romeo, bonjour! There's a French greeting to go with your French trousers. You gave us the slip very neatly last night.
Good morrow to you both. What counterfeit did I give you?
Good morning to you both. How did I give you the slip?
The slip sir, the slip; can you not conceive?
You slipped away, sir, you slipped away. Can't you understand?
Pardon, good Mercutio, my business was great, and in such a case as / mine a man may strain courtesy.
Forgive me, good Mercutio. I had important business, and in a case like mine a man may stretch good manners.
That's as much as to say, such a case as yours constrains a man to bow / in the hams.
That's as good as saying a case like yours forces a man to bend at the knees.
Thou hast most kindly hit it.
Nay, I am the very pink of courtesy.
Yes, I'm the very pink of politeness.
Why, then is my pump well flowered.
Why, then my shoe is well decorated with pinked flowers.
Sure wit, follow me this jest now, till thou hast worn out thy pump, / that when the single sole of it is worn, the jest may remain after the / wearing, solely singular.
Well said! Follow this joke with me now until you've worn out your shoe, so that when its thin sole is worn through, the joke can survive the wearing, unique and on its own.
O single-soled jest, solely singular for the singleness!
Oh, thin-soled joke, unique only in its thinness!
Come between us, good Benvolio; my wits faint.
Come between us, good Benvolio. My wits are fainting.
Swits and spurs, swits and spurs; or I'll cry a match.
Whip and spur your wits, whip and spur! Or I'll claim I've won.
Nay, if thy wits run the wild-goose chase, I am done. For thou hast / more of the wild-goose in one of thy wits, than I am sure, I have in my / whole five. Was I with you there for the goose?

No, if your wits are running a wild-goose chase, I'm finished, because you have more of the wild goose in one of your wits than I have in all five of mine. Was I keeping up with you there on the goose?
Thou wast never with me for anything, when thou wast not there for the / goose.
You never kept up with me for anything when you weren't there as the goose.
I will bite thee by the ear for that jest.
I'll bite your ear for that joke.
Thy wit is a very bitter sweeting, it is a most sharp sauce.
Your wit is a very bitter apple; it's a really sharp sauce.
And is it not then well served in to a sweet goose?
And isn't that the right sauce to serve with a sweet goose?
O here's a wit of cheveril, that stretches from an inch narrow to an / ell broad.
Oh, here's a wit made of kid leather, which stretches from an inch to a yard wide.
I stretch it out for that word broad, which added to the goose, proves / thee far and wide a broad goose.
I stretch it for that word 'broad', which, added to 'goose', proves you're a big fat goose far and wide.

Why, is not this better now than groaning for love? Now art thou / sociable, now art thou Romeo; now art thou what thou art, by art as / well as by nature. For this drivelling love is like a great natural, / that runs lolling up and down to hide his bauble in a hole.

Now, isn't this better than groaning about love? Now you're sociable, now you're Romeo. Now you're what you really are, by training as well as by nature. This drooling love is like a great idiot running up and down with his tongue hanging out, looking for a hole to hide his toy stick in.
Thou desirest me to stop in my tale against the hair.
You want me to stop my tale against my will.
Thou wouldst else have made thy tale large.
Otherwise you'd have made your tale too long.
O, thou art deceived; I would have made it short, for I was come to the / whole depth of my tale, and meant indeed to occupy the argument no / longer.
Oh, you're wrong. I'd have made it short, because I'd reached the whole depth of my tale and didn't intend to stay on the subject any longer.
Here's goodly gear! / A sail, a sail!
Here's a fine sight! A ship, a ship!
Two, two; a shirt and a smock.
Two, two: a man's shirt and a woman's smock.
Good Peter, to hide her face; for her fan's the fairer face.
Good Peter, give it her to hide her face: her fan is the prettier face.
God give you good morning, gentlemen.
God give you good afternoon, lovely lady.
'Tis no less, I tell ye; for the bawdy hand of the dial is now upon the / prick of noon.
It's no earlier, I tell you: the rude hand of the clock is now pointing at noon.
Out upon you! What a man are you?
Get away with you! What kind of man are you?
One, gentlewoman, that God hath made for himself to mar.
One, lady, whom God made for himself to spoil.
By my troth, it is well said; for himself to mar, quoth a? Gentlemen, / can any of you tell me where I may find the young Romeo?
Honestly, that's well said! 'For himself to spoil,' did he say? Gentlemen, can any of you tell me where I can find the young Romeo?
I can tell you: but young Romeo will be older when you have found him / than he was when you sought him. I am the youngest of that name, for / fault of a worse.
I can tell you, but young Romeo will be older when you've found him than he was when you started looking. I'm the youngest of that name, for lack of a worse one.
Yea, is the worst well? Very well took, i'faith; wisely, wisely.
Well? Is the worst well? Very well understood, honestly. Wise, wise.
If you be he, sir, I desire some confidence with you.
If you're him, sir, I'd like a private word with you.
She will endite him to some supper.
She'll invite him to some supper.
A bawd, a bawd, a bawd! So ho!
A bawd, a bawd, a bawd! Tally-ho!
No hare, sir; unless a hare, sir, in a lenten pie, that is something / stale and hoar ere it be spent.
No hare, sir, unless it's a hare in a meatless Lent pie, which is a bit stale and mouldy before it's eaten.

An old hare hoar, / And an old hare hoar, / Is very good meat in Lent; / But a hare that is hoar / Is too much for a score / When it hoars ere it be spent. / Romeo, will you come to your father's? We'll to dinner thither.

An old hare, grey with mould, and an old grey hare, is very good meat in Lent. But a hare that's mouldy is too much to pay for when it goes mouldy before it's eaten. Romeo, are you coming to your father's? We're going there for dinner.
Farewell, ancient lady; farewell, lady, lady, lady.
Goodbye, old lady. Goodbye, lady, lady, lady.
I pray you, sir, what saucy merchant was this that was so full of his / ropery?
Please tell me, sir, who was that cheeky fellow so full of his dirty jokes?
A gentleman, Nurse, that loves to hear himself talk, and will speak / more in a minute than he will stand to in a month.
A gentleman, Nurse, who loves to hear himself talk, and will say more in a minute than he'll stand by in a month.

And a speak anything against me, I'll take him down, and a were lustier / than he is, and twenty such Jacks. And if I cannot, I'll find those / that shall. Scurvy knave! I am none of his flirt-gills; I am none of / his skains-mates.—And thou must stand by too and suffer every knave to / use me at his pleasure!

If he says anything against me, I'll take him down a peg, even if he were stronger than he is, and twenty more rascals like him. And if I can't, I'll find people who can. Rotten scoundrel! I'm not one of his loose women; I'm not one of his gangster friends. And you have to stand by too, and let every scoundrel use me as he likes!

I saw no man use you at his pleasure; if I had, my weapon should / quickly have been out. I warrant you, I dare draw as soon as another / man, if I see occasion in a good quarrel, and the law on my side.

I didn't see any man use you as he likes. If I had, my weapon would have been out quickly, I promise you. I dare draw as quickly as any other man if I see the chance of a good fight, with the law on my side.

Now, afore God, I am so vexed that every part about me quivers. Scurvy / knave. Pray you, sir, a word: and as I told you, my young lady bid me / enquire you out; what she bade me say, I will keep to myself. But first / let me tell ye, if ye should lead her in a fool's paradise, as they / say, it were a very gross kind of behaviour, as they say; for the / gentlewoman is young. And therefore, if you should deal double with / her, truly it were an ill thing to be offered to any gentlewoman, and / very weak dealing.

Now, before God, I'm so upset that every part of me is shaking. Rotten scoundrel! Please, sir, a word. As I told you, my young lady told me to find you. What she told me to say I'll keep to myself. But first let me tell you, if you were to lead her into a fool's paradise, as they say, it would be a very wicked kind of behaviour, as they say, because the young lady is young. And so if you were to deceive her, it would truly be a bad thing to offer any lady, and very shabby behaviour.
Nurse, commend me to thy lady and mistress. I protest unto / thee,—
Nurse, give my regards to your lady and mistress. I swear to you...
Good heart, and i'faith I will tell her as much. Lord, Lord, she will / be a joyful woman.
Bless your heart, and honestly, I'll tell her so. Lord, Lord, she'll be a happy woman.
What wilt thou tell her, Nurse? Thou dost not mark me.
What will you tell her, Nurse? You're not listening to me.
I will tell her, sir, that you do protest, which, as I take it, is a / gentlemanlike offer.
I'll tell her, sir, that you 'swear', which, as I understand it, is a gentlemanly proposal.
Bid her devise / Some means to come to shrift this afternoon, / And there she shall at Friar Lawrence' cell / Be shriv'd and married. Here is for thy pains.
Tell her to find some way of coming to confession this afternoon, and there, at Friar Lawrence's cell, she'll be forgiven and married. Here's something for your trouble.
No truly, sir; not a penny.
No, really, sir, not a penny.
Go to; I say you shall.
Go on, I say you will.
This afternoon, sir? Well, she shall be there.
This afternoon, sir? Well, she'll be there.

And stay, good Nurse, behind the abbey wall. / Within this hour my man shall be with thee, / And bring thee cords made like a tackled stair, / Which to the high topgallant of my joy / Must be my convoy in the secret night. / Farewell, be trusty, and I'll quit thy pains; / Farewell; commend me to thy mistress.

And wait, good Nurse, behind the abbey wall. Within the hour my servant will meet you there and bring you a rope ladder, which will carry me up to the highest point of my joy in the secret night. Goodbye. Be loyal, and I'll reward your trouble. Goodbye. Give my regards to your mistress.
Now God in heaven bless thee. Hark you, sir.
Now God in heaven bless you! Listen, sir.
What say'st thou, my dear Nurse?
What is it, my dear Nurse?
Is your man secret? Did you ne'er hear say, / Two may keep counsel, putting one away?
Can your servant keep a secret? Haven't you heard the saying, 'Two can keep a secret if one of them is out of the way'?
I warrant thee my man's as true as steel.
I promise you my servant is as true as steel.

Well, sir, my mistress is the sweetest lady. Lord, Lord! When 'twas a / little prating thing,—O, there is a nobleman in town, one Paris, that / would fain lay knife aboard; but she, good soul, had as lief see a / toad, a very toad, as see him. I anger her sometimes, and tell her that / Paris is the properer man, but I'll warrant you, when I say so, she / looks as pale as any clout in the versal world. Doth not rosemary and / Romeo begin both with a letter?

Well, sir, my mistress is the sweetest lady. Lord, Lord, when she was a little chattering thing... Oh, there's a nobleman in town, a man called Paris, who'd love to stake his claim on her. But she, good soul, would just as soon see a toad, a real toad, as see him. I make her angry sometimes by telling her Paris is the better-looking man, but I promise you, when I say so, she goes as white as any sheet in the whole world. Don't 'rosemary' and 'Romeo' both begin with the same letter?
Ay, Nurse; what of that? Both with an R.
Yes, Nurse. What of it? Both with an R.

Ah, mocker! That's the dog's name. R is for the—no, I know it begins / with some other letter, and she hath the prettiest sententious of it, / of you and rosemary, that it would do you good to hear it.

Ah, you're teasing! That's the dog's name: R is for the... No, I know it begins with some other letter. And she has the prettiest sayings about it, about you and rosemary, that it would do you good to hear them.
Give my regards to your lady.

The clock struck nine when I did send the Nurse, / In half an hour she promised to return. / Perchance she cannot meet him. That's not so. / O, she is lame. Love's heralds should be thoughts, / Which ten times faster glides than the sun's beams, / Driving back shadows over lowering hills: / Therefore do nimble-pinion'd doves draw love, / And therefore hath the wind-swift Cupid wings. / Now is the sun upon the highmost hill / Of this day's journey, and from nine till twelve / Is three long hours, yet she is not come. / Had she affections and warm youthful blood, / She'd be as swift in motion as a ball; / My words would bandy her to my sweet love, / And his to me. / But old folks, many feign as they were dead; / Unwieldy, slow, heavy and pale as lead.

The clock struck nine when I sent the Nurse, and she promised to come back in half an hour. Perhaps she can't find him. No, that can't be it. Oh, she's lame! Love's messengers should be thoughts, which travel ten times faster than sunbeams chasing shadows off dark hills. That's why nimble-winged doves pull Venus's chariot, and why Cupid, swift as the wind, has wings. Now the sun is at the highest point of today's journey, and from nine until twelve is three long hours, and still she hasn't come. If she had feelings and warm young blood, she'd move as fast as a ball: my words would bat her to my sweet love, and his would bat her back to me. But many old people act as though they were dead: clumsy, slow, heavy and pale as lead.
O God, she comes. O honey Nurse, what news? / Hast thou met with him? Send thy man away.
Oh God, she's coming! Oh, honey Nurse, what news? Have you met him? Send your servant away.
Now, good sweet Nurse,—O Lord, why look'st thou sad? / Though news be sad, yet tell them merrily; / If good, thou sham'st the music of sweet news / By playing it to me with so sour a face.
Now, good sweet Nurse... Oh Lord, why do you look so sad? Even if the news is sad, tell it cheerfully. If it's good, you're ruining the music of sweet news by playing it to me with such a sour face.
I am aweary, give me leave awhile; / Fie, how my bones ache! What a jaunt have I had!
I'm tired. Leave me alone for a while. Oh, how my bones ache! What a trek I've had!
I would thou hadst my bones, and I thy news: / Nay come, I pray thee speak; good, good Nurse, speak.
I wish you had my bones and I had your news. No, come on, please speak. Good, good Nurse, speak.
Jesu, what haste? Can you not stay a while? Do you not see that I am / out of breath?
Jesus, what a hurry! Can't you wait a moment? Don't you see I'm out of breath?

How art thou out of breath, when thou hast breath / To say to me that thou art out of breath? / The excuse that thou dost make in this delay / Is longer than the tale thou dost excuse. / Is thy news good or bad? Answer to that; / Say either, and I'll stay the circumstance. / Let me be satisfied, is't good or bad?

How can you be out of breath when you have the breath to tell me you're out of breath? The excuse you're making for the delay is longer than the story you're delaying. Is your news good or bad? Answer that. Say which, and I'll wait for the details. Satisfy me: is it good or bad?

Well, you have made a simple choice; you know not how to choose a man. / Romeo? No, not he. Though his face be better than any man's, yet his / leg excels all men's, and for a hand and a foot, and a body, though / they be not to be talked on, yet they are past compare. He is not the / flower of courtesy, but I'll warrant him as gentle as a lamb. Go thy / ways, wench, serve God. What, have you dined at home?

Well, you've made a foolish choice. You don't know how to choose a man. Romeo? No, not him. Though his face is better than any man's, his leg is better than all men's, and as for his hand and foot and body, though they're not worth mentioning, they're beyond compare. He isn't the very flower of good manners, but I promise you he's as gentle as a lamb. Off you go, girl, serve God. What, have you had dinner at home?
No, no. But all this did I know before. / What says he of our marriage? What of that?
No, no. But I knew all this already. What does he say about our marriage? What about that?

Lord, how my head aches! What a head have I! / It beats as it would fall in twenty pieces. / My back o' t'other side,—O my back, my back! / Beshrew your heart for sending me about / To catch my death with jauncing up and down.

Lord, how my head aches! What a headache I have! It's pounding as if it would fall into twenty pieces. And my back, on the other side... oh, my back, my back! Curse you for sending me running about to catch my death with trudging up and down!
I'faith, I am sorry that thou art not well. / Sweet, sweet, sweet Nurse, tell me, what says my love?
Honestly, I'm sorry you're not well. Sweet, sweet, sweet Nurse, tell me, what does my love say?
Your love says like an honest gentleman, / And a courteous, and a kind, and a handsome, / And I warrant a virtuous,—Where is your mother?
Your love says, like an honest gentleman, and a polite one, and a kind one, and a handsome one, and I'm sure a virtuous one... Where is your mother?
Where is my mother? Why, she is within. / Where should she be? How oddly thou repliest. / 'Your love says, like an honest gentleman, / 'Where is your mother?'
Where is my mother? Why, she's inside. Where else would she be? What a strange answer! 'Your love says, like an honest gentleman, where is your mother?'
O God's lady dear, / Are you so hot? Marry, come up, I trow. / Is this the poultice for my aching bones? / Henceforward do your messages yourself.
Oh, dear Mother of God! Are you so impatient? Well, really! Is this the medicine for my aching bones? From now on, run your own errands.
Here's such a coil. Come, what says Romeo?
What a fuss! Come on, what does Romeo say?
Have you got leave to go to shrift today?
Have you got permission to go to confession today?

Then hie you hence to Friar Lawrence' cell; / There stays a husband to make you a wife. / Now comes the wanton blood up in your cheeks, / They'll be in scarlet straight at any news. / Hie you to church. I must another way, / To fetch a ladder by the which your love / Must climb a bird's nest soon when it is dark. / I am the drudge, and toil in your delight; / But you shall bear the burden soon at night. / Go. I'll to dinner; hie you to the cell.

Then hurry off to Friar Lawrence's cell. There's a husband waiting there to make you a wife. Now the eager blood is rising in your cheeks: they turn scarlet at any news. Hurry to church. I must go another way, to fetch a ladder that your love will use to climb up to his bird's nest as soon as it's dark. I'm the drudge, working hard for your pleasure, but you'll be the one bearing the weight soon, tonight. Go. I'll go to dinner. Hurry to the cell.
Hie to high fortune! Honest Nurse, farewell.
Hurry to my great good fortune! Honest Nurse, goodbye.
So smile the heavens upon this holy act / That after-hours with sorrow chide us not.
May heaven smile on this holy act, so that the future doesn't punish us with sorrow.

Amen, amen, but come what sorrow can, / It cannot countervail the exchange of joy / That one short minute gives me in her sight. / Do thou but close our hands with holy words, / Then love-devouring death do what he dare, / It is enough I may but call her mine.

Amen, amen. But whatever sorrow comes, it can't outweigh the joy that one short minute in her sight gives me. Just join our hands with holy words, and then let love-devouring death do whatever it dares: it's enough that I can call her mine.

These violent delights have violent ends, / And in their triumph die; like fire and powder, / Which as they kiss consume. The sweetest honey / Is loathsome in his own deliciousness, / And in the taste confounds the appetite. / Therefore love moderately: long love doth so; / Too swift arrives as tardy as too slow.

These violent delights have violent ends, and die in their moment of triumph, like fire and gunpowder, which destroy each other as they kiss. The sweetest honey becomes sickening because it's so delicious, and tasting it destroys the appetite. So love moderately: that's what long-lasting love does. Going too fast gets you there as late as going too slowly.
Here comes the lady. O, so light a foot / Will ne'er wear out the everlasting flint. / A lover may bestride the gossamers / That idles in the wanton summer air / And yet not fall; so light is vanity.

Here comes the lady. Oh, such a light foot will never wear out the everlasting stone floor. A lover could stand on the spiders' threads that float in the playful summer air and still not fall, so light are earthly pleasures.
Good even to my ghostly confessor.
Good evening to my holy confessor.
Romeo shall thank thee, daughter, for us both.
Romeo will thank you, daughter, for both of us.
As much to him, else is his thanks too much.
I'll give him the same greeting, or his thanks would be more than I deserve.

Ah, Juliet, if the measure of thy joy / Be heap'd like mine, and that thy skill be more / To blazon it, then sweeten with thy breath / This neighbour air, and let rich music's tongue / Unfold the imagin'd happiness that both / Receive in either by this dear encounter.

Ah, Juliet, if your joy is heaped as high as mine, and you have more skill to describe it, then sweeten the air around us with your breath, and let the rich music of your voice describe the happiness we both imagine, which each of us receives from the other in this dear meeting.

Conceit more rich in matter than in words, / Brags of his substance, not of ornament. / They are but beggars that can count their worth; / But my true love is grown to such excess, / I cannot sum up sum of half my wealth.

True understanding, richer in substance than in words, is proud of what it is, not of how it is decorated. People who can count their wealth are only beggars, but my true love has grown so great that I can't add up even half of my riches.
Come, come with me, and we will make short work, / For, by your leaves, you shall not stay alone / Till holy church incorporate two in one.
Come, come with me, and we'll make quick work of this. With your permission, you won't be left alone together until holy church has made the two of you one.
I pray thee, good Mercutio, let's retire: / The day is hot, the Capulets abroad, / And if we meet, we shall not scape a brawl, / For now these hot days, is the mad blood stirring.
Please, good Mercutio, let's go home. The day is hot, the Capulets are out, and if we meet we won't avoid a fight, because in this hot weather people's blood is up.

Thou art like one of these fellows that, when he enters the confines of / a tavern, claps me his sword upon the table, and says 'God send me no / need of thee!' and by the operation of the second cup draws him on the / drawer, when indeed there is no need.

You're like one of those men who, as soon as he walks into a tavern, slaps his sword on the table and says 'God grant I won't need you!', and by the time the second drink has worked on him, draws it on the waiter, when there's really no need.
Am I like such a fellow?
Come, come, thou art as hot a Jack in thy mood as any in Italy; and as / soon moved to be moody, and as soon moody to be moved.
Come on, you're as hot-tempered a fellow as any in Italy, as quickly provoked into a temper, and as quick-tempered when provoked.

Nay, an there were two such, we should have none shortly, for one would / kill the other. Thou? Why, thou wilt quarrel with a man that hath a / hair more or a hair less in his beard than thou hast. Thou wilt quarrel / with a man for cracking nuts, having no other reason but because thou / hast hazel eyes. What eye but such an eye would spy out such a quarrel? / Thy head is as full of quarrels as an egg is full of meat, and yet thy / head hath been beaten as addle as an egg for quarrelling. Thou hast / quarrelled with a man for coughing in the street, because he hath / wakened thy dog that hath lain asleep in the sun. Didst thou not fall / out with a tailor for wearing his new doublet before Easter? with / another for tying his new shoes with an old riband? And yet thou wilt / tutor me from quarrelling!

Why, if there were two like you, we'd soon have none, because one would kill the other. You? You'd quarrel with a man for having one hair more or one hair less in his beard than you have. You'd quarrel with a man for cracking nuts, for no other reason than that you have hazel eyes. What eye but an eye like that would spot a quarrel like that? Your head is as full of quarrels as an egg is full of food, and yet it's been beaten as scrambled as an egg for quarrelling. You quarrelled with a man for coughing in the street because he woke your dog that was asleep in the sun. Didn't you fall out with a tailor for wearing his new jacket before Easter? And with another for tying his new shoes with old laces? And yet you'd teach me not to quarrel!
And I were so apt to quarrel as thou art, any man should buy the fee / simple of my life for an hour and a quarter.
If I were as quick to quarrel as you are, anyone could buy my life outright for an hour and a quarter's purchase.
By my head, here comes the Capulets.
By my head, here come the Capulets.
By my heel, I care not.
By my heel, I don't care.
Follow me close, for I will speak to them. / Gentlemen, good-den: a word with one of you.
Follow close behind me, because I'm going to speak to them. Gentlemen, good afternoon. A word with one of you.
And but one word with one of us? Couple it with something; make it a / word and a blow.
Just one word with one of us? Pair it with something: make it a word and a blow.
You shall find me apt enough to that, sir, and you will give me / occasion.
You'll find me quite ready for that, sir, if you give me a reason.
Could you not take some occasion without giving?
Couldn't you find a reason without being given one?
Mercutio, you keep company with Romeo.
Consort? What, dost thou make us minstrels? And thou make minstrels of / us, look to hear nothing but discords. Here's my fiddlestick, here's / that shall make you dance. Zounds, consort!

'Keep company'? What, are you calling us a band of minstrels? If you're making minstrels of us, expect to hear nothing but harsh noise. Here's my fiddle bow: here's what will make you dance. God's wounds, 'keep company'!
We talk here in the public haunt of men. / Either withdraw unto some private place, / And reason coldly of your grievances, / Or else depart; here all eyes gaze on us.
We're talking here in a public place. Either go somewhere private and discuss your grievances calmly, or else leave. Here everyone is staring at us.
Men's eyes were made to look, and let them gaze. / I will not budge for no man's pleasure, I.
Men's eyes were made to look, so let them stare. I won't move to please anyone, not I.
Well, peace be with you, sir, here comes my man.
Well, peace be with you, sir. Here comes my man.
But I'll be hanged, sir, if he wear your livery. / Marry, go before to field, he'll be your follower; / Your worship in that sense may call him man.
I'll be hanged, sir, if he's wearing your uniform. Indeed, go to the duelling ground first and he'll follow you: in that sense your worship can call him your man.
Romeo, the love I bear thee can afford / No better term than this: Thou art a villain.
Romeo, the love I have for you can find no better word than this: you are a villain.
Tybalt, the reason that I have to love thee / Doth much excuse the appertaining rage / To such a greeting. Villain am I none; / Therefore farewell; I see thou know'st me not.
Tybalt, the reason I have to love you excuses the rage that ought to meet such a greeting. I am no villain. So goodbye: I can see you don't know me.
Boy, this shall not excuse the injuries / That thou hast done me, therefore turn and draw.
Boy, this won't excuse the injuries you've done me. So turn and draw your sword.

I do protest I never injur'd thee, / But love thee better than thou canst devise / Till thou shalt know the reason of my love. / And so good Capulet, which name I tender / As dearly as mine own, be satisfied.
I swear I never injured you, and I love you more than you can imagine, until you know the reason for my love. And so, good Capulet, a name I value as dearly as my own, be satisfied.
O calm, dishonourable, vile submission! / [Draws] Alla stoccata carries it away. / Tybalt, you rat-catcher, will you walk?
Oh calm, dishonourable, contemptible surrender! 'Alla stoccata', the fancy thrust, wins the day. Tybalt, you rat-catcher, will you step aside with me?
What wouldst thou have with me?
What do you want with me?

Good King of Cats, nothing but one of your nine lives; that I mean to / make bold withal, and, as you shall use me hereafter, dry-beat the rest / of the eight. Will you pluck your sword out of his pilcher by the ears? / Make haste, lest mine be about your ears ere it be out.

Good King of Cats, nothing but one of your nine lives. I intend to take that one, and, depending on how you treat me afterwards, thrash the other eight. Will you pull your sword out of its scabbard by the ears? Hurry, or mine will be round your ears before yours is out.
Gentle Mercutio, put thy rapier up.
Gentle Mercutio, put your sword away.
Come on, sir, let's see your passado.

Draw, Benvolio; beat down their weapons. / Gentlemen, for shame, forbear this outrage, / Tybalt, Mercutio, the Prince expressly hath / Forbid this bandying in Verona streets. / Hold, Tybalt! Good Mercutio!

Draw, Benvolio, and beat down their weapons. Gentlemen, for shame, stop this violence! Tybalt, Mercutio, the Prince has expressly forbidden fighting in the streets of Verona. Stop, Tybalt! Good Mercutio!
I am hurt. / A plague o' both your houses. I am sped. / Is he gone, and hath nothing?
I'm hurt. A plague on both your houses! I'm finished. Has he gone, without a scratch?
Ay, ay, a scratch, a scratch. Marry, 'tis enough. / Where is my page? Go villain, fetch a surgeon.
Yes, yes, a scratch, a scratch. Indeed, it's enough. Where's my page? Go, boy, fetch a surgeon.
Courage, man; the hurt cannot be much.
Courage, man. The wound can't be much.

No, 'tis not so deep as a well, nor so wide as a church door, but 'tis / enough, 'twill serve. Ask for me tomorrow, and you shall find me a / grave man. I am peppered, I warrant, for this world. A plague o' both / your houses. Zounds, a dog, a rat, a mouse, a cat, to scratch a man to / death. A braggart, a rogue, a villain, that fights by the book of / arithmetic!—Why the devil came you between us? I was hurt under your / arm.

No, it's not as deep as a well, or as wide as a church door, but it's enough. It'll do. Ask for me tomorrow and you'll find me a grave man. I'm done for in this world, I promise you. A plague on both your houses! God's wounds, a dog, a rat, a mouse, a cat, to scratch a man to death! A braggart, a rogue, a villain who fights by the textbook! Why the devil did you come between us? I was hurt under your arm.
I thought all for the best.
I meant it for the best.
Help me into some house, Benvolio, / Or I shall faint. A plague o' both your houses. / They have made worms' meat of me. / I have it, and soundly too. Your houses!
Help me into some house, Benvolio, or I'll faint. A plague on both your houses! They've made me into food for worms. I've got it, and properly too. Your houses!

This gentleman, the Prince's near ally, / My very friend, hath got his mortal hurt / In my behalf; my reputation stain'd / With Tybalt's slander,—Tybalt, that an hour / Hath been my cousin. O sweet Juliet, / Thy beauty hath made me effeminate / And in my temper soften'd valour's steel.

This gentleman, the Prince's close relative and my true friend, has been fatally wounded on my behalf, and my reputation is stained by Tybalt's insult: Tybalt, who for an hour has been my cousin! Oh sweet Juliet, your beauty has made me womanish and softened the steel of courage in my character.
O Romeo, Romeo, brave Mercutio's dead, / That gallant spirit hath aspir'd the clouds, / Which too untimely here did scorn the earth.
Oh Romeo, Romeo, brave Mercutio is dead! That gallant spirit has risen up to the clouds, after scorning the earth too early.
This day's black fate on mo days doth depend; / This but begins the woe others must end.
This day's black fate hangs over more days to come. This only begins the misery that other days must finish.
Here comes the furious Tybalt back again.
Here comes the furious Tybalt back again.

Again in triumph, and Mercutio slain? / Away to heaven respective lenity, / And fire-ey'd fury be my conduct now! / Now, Tybalt, take the 'villain' back again / That late thou gav'st me, for Mercutio's soul / Is but a little way above our heads, / Staying for thine to keep him company. / Either thou or I, or both, must go with him.

Back again in triumph, and Mercutio dead? Away to heaven with considerate mildness, and let fiery-eyed fury guide me now! Now, Tybalt, take back the 'villain' you gave me just now, because Mercutio's soul is only a little way above our heads, waiting for yours to keep it company. Either you or I, or both of us, must go with him.
Thou wretched boy, that didst consort him here, / Shalt with him hence.
You miserable boy, you kept him company here, and you'll go with him from here.
Romeo, away, be gone! / The citizens are up, and Tybalt slain. / Stand not amaz'd. The Prince will doom thee death / If thou art taken. Hence, be gone, away!
Romeo, go, get away! The citizens are roused, and Tybalt is dead. Don't stand there stunned. The Prince will sentence you to death if you're caught. Go, get away, go!
Which way ran he that kill'd Mercutio? / Tybalt, that murderer, which way ran he?
Which way did the man who killed Mercutio run? Tybalt, that murderer, which way did he run?
Up, sir, go with me. / I charge thee in the Prince's name obey.
Get up, sir, come with me. I order you in the Prince's name to obey.
Where are the vile beginners of this fray?
Where are the wicked people who started this fight?
O noble Prince, I can discover all / The unlucky manage of this fatal brawl. / There lies the man, slain by young Romeo, / That slew thy kinsman, brave Mercutio.
Oh noble Prince, I can reveal everything about how this deadly fight unluckily happened. There lies the man, killed by young Romeo, who killed your relative, brave Mercutio.
Tybalt, my cousin! O my brother's child! / O Prince! O husband! O, the blood is spill'd / Of my dear kinsman! Prince, as thou art true, / For blood of ours shed blood of Montague. / O cousin, cousin.
Tybalt, my nephew! Oh, my brother's child! Oh Prince! Oh husband! Oh, my dear relative's blood has been spilled! Prince, if you are just, shed Montague blood for our blood. Oh nephew, nephew!
Benvolio, who began this bloody fray?
Benvolio, who started this bloody fight?

Tybalt, here slain, whom Romeo's hand did slay; / Romeo, that spoke him fair, bid him bethink / How nice the quarrel was, and urg'd withal / Your high displeasure. All this uttered / With gentle breath, calm look, knees humbly bow'd / Could not take truce with the unruly spleen / Of Tybalt, deaf to peace, but that he tilts / With piercing steel at bold Mercutio's breast, / Who, all as hot, turns deadly point to point, / And, with a martial scorn, with one hand beats / Cold death aside, and with the other sends / It back to Tybalt, whose dexterity / Retorts it. Romeo he cries aloud, / 'Hold, friends! Friends, part!' and swifter than his tongue, / His agile arm beats down their fatal points, / And 'twixt them rushes; underneath whose arm / An envious thrust from Tybalt hit the life / Of stout Mercutio, and then Tybalt fled. / But by and by comes back to Romeo, / Who had but newly entertain'd revenge, / And to't they go like lightning; for, ere I / Could draw to part them was stout Tybalt slain; / And as he fell did Romeo turn and fly. / This is the truth, or let Benvolio die.

Tybalt, lying here, killed by Romeo's hand. Romeo spoke politely to him, told him to consider how trivial the quarrel was, and reminded him of your great anger too. All this, said gently, with a calm face and humbly bent knee, couldn't make peace with the wild temper of Tybalt, who was deaf to peace. He thrust his piercing sword at bold Mercutio's chest. Mercutio, just as hot-tempered, met point with deadly point, and with a soldier's scorn beat cold death aside with one hand and sent it back at Tybalt with the other, and Tybalt skilfully returned it. Romeo shouted, 'Stop, friends! Friends, separate!' and faster than his tongue, his quick arm beat down their deadly swords and he rushed between them. Under his arm a spiteful thrust from Tybalt took the life of brave Mercutio, and then Tybalt ran away. But soon he came back to Romeo, who had only just begun to think of revenge, and they went at it like lightning. Before I could draw to separate them, brave Tybalt was killed, and as he fell, Romeo turned and ran. This is the truth, or let Benvolio die.

He is a kinsman to the Montague. / Affection makes him false, he speaks not true. / Some twenty of them fought in this black strife, / And all those twenty could but kill one life. / I beg for justice, which thou, Prince, must give; / Romeo slew Tybalt, Romeo must not live.

He's a relative of the Montagues. Affection makes him lie; he isn't telling the truth. Some twenty of them fought in this dark fight, and all twenty could only kill one life. I beg for justice, which you, Prince, must give. Romeo killed Tybalt; Romeo must not live.
Romeo slew him, he slew Mercutio. / Who now the price of his dear blood doth owe?
Romeo killed him, and he killed Mercutio. Who now must pay the price for Mercutio's dear blood?
Not Romeo, Prince, he was Mercutio's friend; / His fault concludes but what the law should end, / The life of Tybalt.
Not Romeo, Prince. He was Mercutio's friend. His crime only finished what the law would have done anyway: taking Tybalt's life.

And for that offence / Immediately we do exile him hence. / I have an interest in your hate's proceeding, / My blood for your rude brawls doth lie a-bleeding. / But I'll amerce you with so strong a fine / That you shall all repent the loss of mine. / I will be deaf to pleading and excuses; / Nor tears nor prayers shall purchase out abuses. / Therefore use none. Let Romeo hence in haste, / Else, when he is found, that hour is his last. / Bear hence this body, and attend our will. / Mercy but murders, pardoning those that kill.

And for that offence I exile him from here, at once. Your feud concerns me now: my own blood lies bleeding because of your savage fights. But I'll punish you with such a heavy fine that you'll all regret the loss of my relative. I'll be deaf to pleas and excuses. Neither tears nor prayers will buy pardon for these crimes, so don't use any. Let Romeo leave quickly, or else the hour he is found will be his last. Carry this body away, and await my judgement. Mercy only commits murder when it pardons those who kill.

Gallop apace, you fiery-footed steeds, / Towards Phoebus' lodging. Such a waggoner / As Phaeton would whip you to the west / And bring in cloudy night immediately. / Spread thy close curtain, love-performing night, / That runaway's eyes may wink, and Romeo / Leap to these arms, untalk'd of and unseen. / Lovers can see to do their amorous rites / By their own beauties: or, if love be blind, / It best agrees with night. Come, civil night, / Thou sober-suited matron, all in black, / And learn me how to lose a winning match, / Play'd for a pair of stainless maidenhoods. / Hood my unmann'd blood, bating in my cheeks, / With thy black mantle, till strange love, grow bold, / Think true love acted simple modesty. / Come, night, come Romeo; come, thou day in night; / For thou wilt lie upon the wings of night / Whiter than new snow upon a raven's back. / Come gentle night, come loving black-brow'd night, / Give me my Romeo, and when I shall die, / Take him and cut him out in little stars, / And he will make the face of heaven so fine / That all the world will be in love with night, / And pay no worship to the garish sun. / O, I have bought the mansion of a love, / But not possess'd it; and though I am sold, / Not yet enjoy'd. So tedious is this day / As is the night before some festival / To an impatient child that hath new robes / And may not wear them. O, here comes my Nurse, / And she brings news, and every tongue that speaks / But Romeo's name speaks heavenly eloquence.

Gallop fast, you fiery-footed horses, towards the sun god's home in the west. A driver like Phaeton would whip you westwards and bring cloudy night at once. Spread your thick curtain, night, when love is made, so that prying eyes may close and Romeo can leap into these arms, unseen and unspoken of. Lovers can see to perform their loving rites by the light of their own beauty; or, if love is blind, it suits the night best. Come, gentle night, you soberly dressed lady, all in black, and teach me how to lose a game I'll win by losing, played for a pair of spotless virginities. Hide the wild blood fluttering in my cheeks with your black cloak, until shy love grows bold and thinks the act of true love is simple innocence. Come, night! Come, Romeo! Come, you day in the night, because you'll lie on the wings of night whiter than new snow on a raven's back. Come, gentle night; come, loving, black-browed night. Give me my Romeo, and when I die, take him and cut him out in little stars, and he'll make the face of heaven so beautiful that all the world will fall in love with night and stop worshipping the gaudy sun. Oh, I've bought the mansion of a love but haven't moved in, and though I've been sold, I haven't yet been enjoyed. This day is as tedious as the night before a festival to an impatient child who has new clothes and isn't allowed to wear them. Oh, here comes my Nurse, and she brings news. Every voice that speaks just Romeo's name speaks with heavenly eloquence.
Now, Nurse, what news? What hast thou there? / The cords that Romeo bid thee fetch?
Now, Nurse, what news? What have you got there? The ropes Romeo told you to fetch?
Ay me, what news? Why dost thou wring thy hands?
Oh no, what's the news? Why are you wringing your hands?
Ah, well-a-day, he's dead, he's dead, he's dead! / We are undone, lady, we are undone. / Alack the day, he's gone, he's kill'd, he's dead.
Oh, alas, he's dead, he's dead, he's dead! We're ruined, lady, we're ruined! Oh, what a day! He's gone, he's killed, he's dead!
Romeo can, / Though heaven cannot. O Romeo, Romeo. / Who ever would have thought it? Romeo!
Romeo can, though heaven can't. Oh Romeo, Romeo! Who would ever have thought it? Romeo!

What devil art thou, that dost torment me thus? / This torture should be roar'd in dismal hell. / Hath Romeo slain himself? Say thou but Ay, / And that bare vowel I shall poison more / Than the death-darting eye of cockatrice. / I am not I if there be such an I; / Or those eyes shut that make thee answer Ay. / If he be slain, say Ay; or if not, No. / Brief sounds determine of my weal or woe.

What kind of devil are you, to torment me like this? This torture should be howled in miserable hell. Has Romeo killed himself? Just say 'Yes', and that simple 'I' will poison me more than the deadly glance of the mythical cockatrice. I won't be myself if there is such an 'Ay', or if his eyes are shut, which would make you answer 'Ay'. If he's been killed, say 'Ay'; if not, 'No'. Short sounds will decide my happiness or misery.

I saw the wound, I saw it with mine eyes, / God save the mark!—here on his manly breast. / A piteous corse, a bloody piteous corse; / Pale, pale as ashes, all bedaub'd in blood, / All in gore-blood. I swounded at the sight.

I saw the wound, I saw it with my own eyes (God forgive me for saying it), here on his manly chest. A pitiful corpse, a bloody, pitiful corpse, pale, pale as ashes, all smeared with blood, all clotted blood. I fainted at the sight.
O, break, my heart. Poor bankrout, break at once. / To prison, eyes; ne'er look on liberty. / Vile earth to earth resign; end motion here, / And thou and Romeo press one heavy bier.

Oh, break, my heart! Poor bankrupt heart, break at once! Go to prison, eyes: never look at freedom again. Vile body, give yourself back to the earth, stop moving here, and lie with Romeo on one heavy funeral stretcher.
O Tybalt, Tybalt, the best friend I had. / O courteous Tybalt, honest gentleman! / That ever I should live to see thee dead.
Oh Tybalt, Tybalt, the best friend I had! Oh polite Tybalt, honest gentleman! That I should live to see you dead!

What storm is this that blows so contrary? / Is Romeo slaughter'd and is Tybalt dead? / My dearest cousin, and my dearer lord? / Then dreadful trumpet sound the general doom, / For who is living, if those two are gone?

What storm is this, blowing in opposite directions? Is Romeo killed, and is Tybalt dead? My dearest cousin, and my dearer husband? Then let the dreadful trumpet announce the end of the world, because who is alive if those two are gone?
Tybalt is gone, and Romeo banished, / Romeo that kill'd him, he is banished.
Tybalt is gone and Romeo is banished. Romeo, who killed him, is banished.
O God! Did Romeo's hand shed Tybalt's blood?
Oh God! Did Romeo's hand shed Tybalt's blood?
It did, it did; alas the day, it did.
It did, it did. Oh, what a day, it did!

O serpent heart, hid with a flowering face! / Did ever dragon keep so fair a cave? / Beautiful tyrant, fiend angelical, / Dove-feather'd raven, wolvish-ravening lamb! / Despised substance of divinest show! / Just opposite to what thou justly seem'st, / A damned saint, an honourable villain! / O nature, what hadst thou to do in hell / When thou didst bower the spirit of a fiend / In mortal paradise of such sweet flesh? / Was ever book containing such vile matter / So fairly bound? O, that deceit should dwell / In such a gorgeous palace.

Oh, a snake's heart hidden behind a face like a flower! Did a dragon ever live in such a beautiful cave? Beautiful tyrant! Angelic devil! Raven with a dove's feathers! Lamb that hunts like a wolf! Hateful reality with a most divine appearance! The exact opposite of what you rightly seem: a damned saint, an honourable villain! Oh nature, what were you doing in hell when you housed the spirit of a devil in the earthly paradise of such sweet flesh? Was a book containing such evil ever so beautifully bound? Oh, that deceit should live in such a gorgeous palace!

There's no trust, / No faith, no honesty in men. All perjur'd, / All forsworn, all naught, all dissemblers. / Ah, where's my man? Give me some aqua vitae. / These griefs, these woes, these sorrows make me old. / Shame come to Romeo.

There's no trust, no faith, no honesty in men. They all lie, all break their oaths, all are worthless, all are hypocrites. Ah, where's my servant? Give me some brandy. These griefs, these miseries, these sorrows make me old. Shame on Romeo!

Blister'd be thy tongue / For such a wish! He was not born to shame. / Upon his brow shame is asham'd to sit; / For 'tis a throne where honour may be crown'd / Sole monarch of the universal earth. / O, what a beast was I to chide at him!

May your tongue be blistered for such a wish! He wasn't born for shame. Shame would be ashamed to sit on his brow, because it's a throne where honour may be crowned sole king of the whole earth. Oh, what a beast I was to rage at him!
Will you speak well of him that kill'd your cousin?
Will you speak well of the man who killed your cousin?

Shall I speak ill of him that is my husband? / Ah, poor my lord, what tongue shall smooth thy name, / When I thy three-hours' wife have mangled it? / But wherefore, villain, didst thou kill my cousin? / That villain cousin would have kill'd my husband. / Back, foolish tears, back to your native spring, / Your tributary drops belong to woe, / Which you mistaking offer up to joy. / My husband lives, that Tybalt would have slain, / And Tybalt's dead, that would have slain my husband. / All this is comfort; wherefore weep I then? / Some word there was, worser than Tybalt's death, / That murder'd me. I would forget it fain, / But O, it presses to my memory / Like damned guilty deeds to sinners' minds. / Tybalt is dead, and Romeo banished. / That 'banished,' that one word 'banished,' / Hath slain ten thousand Tybalts. Tybalt's death / Was woe enough, if it had ended there. / Or if sour woe delights in fellowship, / And needly will be rank'd with other griefs, / Why follow'd not, when she said Tybalt's dead, / Thy father or thy mother, nay or both, / Which modern lamentation might have mov'd? / But with a rear-ward following Tybalt's death, / 'Romeo is banished'—to speak that word / Is father, mother, Tybalt, Romeo, Juliet, / All slain, all dead. Romeo is banished, / There is no end, no limit, measure, bound, / In that word's death, no words can that woe sound. / Where is my father and my mother, Nurse?

Should I speak badly of the man who is my husband? Ah, my poor lord, whose tongue will soothe your name when I, your wife of three hours, have torn it apart? But why, you villain, did you kill my cousin? Because that villain cousin would have killed my husband. Back, foolish tears, back to where you came from. Your drops should be paid to grief, but you're mistakenly offering them to joy. My husband is alive, whom Tybalt would have killed, and Tybalt is dead, who would have killed my husband. All this is comforting, so why am I crying? There was some word worse than Tybalt's death that murdered me. I'd gladly forget it, but oh, it forces itself on my memory like damned guilty deeds on sinners' minds. 'Tybalt is dead, and Romeo banished.' That 'banished', that one word 'banished', has killed ten thousand Tybalts. Tybalt's death was misery enough, if it had ended there. Or if bitter misery loves company and has to come with other griefs, why didn't 'your father' or 'your mother', or even both, follow when she said 'Tybalt's dead'? That would have caused ordinary grief. But following Tybalt's death, like a rearguard, came 'Romeo is banished'. To say that word is to say father, mother, Tybalt, Romeo, Juliet are all killed, all dead. 'Romeo is banished': there's no end, no limit, no measure, no boundary to the death in that word. No words can express that misery. Where are my father and mother, Nurse?
Weeping and wailing over Tybalt's corse. / Will you go to them? I will bring you thither.
Weeping and wailing over Tybalt's body. Will you go to them? I'll take you there.

Wash they his wounds with tears. Mine shall be spent, / When theirs are dry, for Romeo's banishment. / Take up those cords. Poor ropes, you are beguil'd, / Both you and I; for Romeo is exil'd. / He made you for a highway to my bed, / But I, a maid, die maiden-widowed. / Come cords, come Nurse, I'll to my wedding bed, / And death, not Romeo, take my maidenhead.

Let them wash his wounds with their tears. When theirs are dry, I'll spend mine on Romeo's banishment. Pick up those ropes. Poor ropes, you've been cheated, both you and I, because Romeo is exiled. He made you to be a highway to my bed, but I'll die a virgin and a widow. Come, ropes; come, Nurse. I'll go to my wedding bed, and let death, not Romeo, take my virginity.
Hie to your chamber. I'll find Romeo / To comfort you. I wot well where he is. / Hark ye, your Romeo will be here at night. / I'll to him, he is hid at Lawrence' cell.
Hurry to your room. I'll find Romeo to comfort you. I know exactly where he is. Listen, your Romeo will be here tonight. I'll go to him: he's hiding at Friar Lawrence's cell.
O find him, give this ring to my true knight, / And bid him come to take his last farewell.
Oh, find him! Give this ring to my true knight, and tell him to come and say his last goodbye.
Romeo, come forth; come forth, thou fearful man. / Affliction is enanmour'd of thy parts / And thou art wedded to calamity.
Romeo, come out. Come out, you frightened man. Suffering has fallen in love with you, and you're married to disaster.
Father, what news? What is the Prince's doom? / What sorrow craves acquaintance at my hand, / That I yet know not?
Father, what news? What is the Prince's sentence? What new sorrow wants to make my acquaintance that I don't know yet?
Too familiar / Is my dear son with such sour company. / I bring thee tidings of the Prince's doom.
My dear son is too familiar with such bitter company. I've brought you news of the Prince's sentence.
What less than doomsday is the Prince's doom?
What can the Prince's sentence be but doomsday, death?
A gentler judgment vanish'd from his lips, / Not body's death, but body's banishment.
A gentler judgement came from his lips: not your body's death, but your body's banishment.
Ha, banishment? Be merciful, say death; / For exile hath more terror in his look, / Much more than death. Do not say banishment.
Ha, banishment? Be merciful: say 'death'. Exile looks more terrifying, much more than death. Don't say 'banishment'.
Hence from Verona art thou banished. / Be patient, for the world is broad and wide.
You are banished from Verona. Be patient: the world is broad and wide.

There is no world without Verona walls, / But purgatory, torture, hell itself. / Hence banished is banish'd from the world, / And world's exile is death. Then banished / Is death misterm'd. Calling death banished, / Thou cutt'st my head off with a golden axe, / And smilest upon the stroke that murders me.

There's no world outside Verona's walls, only purgatory, torture, hell itself. To be banished from here is to be banished from the world, and exile from the world is death. So 'banished' is just death called by the wrong name. By calling death 'banished', you're cutting my head off with a golden axe and smiling at the blow that murders me.

O deadly sin, O rude unthankfulness! / Thy fault our law calls death, but the kind Prince, / Taking thy part, hath brush'd aside the law, / And turn'd that black word death to banishment. / This is dear mercy, and thou see'st it not.

Oh deadly sin! Oh coarse ungratefulness! Our law punishes your crime with death, but the kind Prince, taking your side, has brushed the law aside and changed that black word 'death' into 'banishment'. This is precious mercy, and you can't see it.

'Tis torture, and not mercy. Heaven is here / Where Juliet lives, and every cat and dog, / And little mouse, every unworthy thing, / Live here in heaven and may look on her, / But Romeo may not. More validity, / More honourable state, more courtship lives / In carrion flies than Romeo. They may seize / On the white wonder of dear Juliet's hand, / And steal immortal blessing from her lips, / Who, even in pure and vestal modesty / Still blush, as thinking their own kisses sin. / But Romeo may not, he is banished. / This may flies do, when I from this must fly. / They are free men but I am banished. / And say'st thou yet that exile is not death? / Hadst thou no poison mix'd, no sharp-ground knife, / No sudden mean of death, though ne'er so mean, / But banished to kill me? Banished? / O Friar, the damned use that word in hell. / Howling attends it. How hast thou the heart, / Being a divine, a ghostly confessor, / A sin-absolver, and my friend profess'd, / To mangle me with that word banished?

It's torture, not mercy. Heaven is here, where Juliet lives. Every cat and dog and little mouse, every worthless thing, lives here in heaven and can look at her, but Romeo can't. Flies feeding on dead flesh have more value, more honour, more chance to court her than Romeo. They can land on the white wonder of dear Juliet's hand and steal heavenly blessings from her lips, which, in their pure, virgin modesty, are always blushing, as though they think it a sin when they touch each other. But Romeo can't: he is banished. Flies can do this, while I must fly from it. They are free men, but I am banished. And do you still say exile isn't death? Didn't you have any poison mixed, any sharpened knife, any quick way to die, however low, except 'banished' to kill me with? 'Banished'? Oh Friar, the damned use that word in hell, and howling goes with it. How can you have the heart, being a priest, a holy confessor, a forgiver of sins and my sworn friend, to mangle me with that word 'banished'?
Thou fond mad man, hear me speak a little,
You foolish madman, listen to me for a moment.
O, thou wilt speak again of banishment.
Oh, you'll talk about banishment again.
I'll give thee armour to keep off that word, / Adversity's sweet milk, philosophy, / To comfort thee, though thou art banished.
I'll give you armour to protect you from that word: philosophy, the sweet milk of hard times, to comfort you, even though you are banished.
Yet banished? Hang up philosophy. / Unless philosophy can make a Juliet, / Displant a town, reverse a Prince's doom, / It helps not, it prevails not, talk no more.
'Banished' again? Hang philosophy! Unless philosophy can make a Juliet, move a town or reverse a Prince's sentence, it's no help, it's no use. Don't say any more.
O, then I see that mad men have no ears.
Oh, then I see that madmen have no ears.
How should they, when that wise men have no eyes?
How should they, when wise men have no eyes?
Let me dispute with thee of thy estate.
Let me discuss your situation with you.

Thou canst not speak of that thou dost not feel. / Wert thou as young as I, Juliet thy love, / An hour but married, Tybalt murdered, / Doting like me, and like me banished, / Then mightst thou speak, then mightst thou tear thy hair, / And fall upon the ground as I do now, / Taking the measure of an unmade grave.

You can't talk about what you don't feel. If you were as young as me, with Juliet as your love, married only an hour, Tybalt murdered, as madly in love as me and banished like me, then you could speak. Then you could tear your hair and fall on the ground, as I do now, measuring myself for a grave that hasn't been dug.
Arise; one knocks. Good Romeo, hide thyself.
Get up. Someone's knocking. Good Romeo, hide yourself.
Not I, unless the breath of heartsick groans / Mist-like infold me from the search of eyes.
Not me, unless the breath of my heartsick groans wraps round me like a mist and hides me from searching eyes.
Hark, how they knock!—Who's there?—Romeo, arise, / Thou wilt be taken.—Stay awhile.—Stand up.
Listen how they knock! Who's there? Romeo, get up, you'll be arrested! Wait a moment! Stand up!
Run to my study.—By-and-by.—God's will, / What simpleness is this.—I come, I come.
Run to my study! In a minute! God's will, what foolishness is this? I'm coming, I'm coming!
Who knocks so hard? Whence come you, what's your will?
Who's knocking so hard? Where do you come from? What do you want?
[Within] Let me come in, and you shall know my errand. / I come from Lady Juliet.
Let me come in, and you'll find out my errand. I come from Lady Juliet.
O holy Friar, O, tell me, holy Friar, / Where is my lady's lord, where's Romeo?
Oh holy Friar, oh tell me, holy Friar, where is my lady's husband? Where is Romeo?
There on the ground, with his own tears made drunk.
There on the ground, drunk on his own tears.

O, he is even in my mistress' case. / Just in her case! O woeful sympathy! / Piteous predicament. Even so lies she, / Blubbering and weeping, weeping and blubbering. / Stand up, stand up; stand, and you be a man. / For Juliet's sake, for her sake, rise and stand. / Why should you fall into so deep an O?

Oh, he's in exactly the same state as my mistress, just the same! Oh, what a sad match! What a pitiful situation! She's lying just like that, blubbering and weeping, weeping and blubbering. Stand up, stand up! Stand, if you're a man. For Juliet's sake, for her sake, get up and stand. Why should you fall into such a deep groan?
Ah sir, ah sir, death's the end of all.
Ah, sir, ah, sir, death is the end of everything.

Spakest thou of Juliet? How is it with her? / Doth not she think me an old murderer, / Now I have stain'd the childhood of our joy / With blood remov'd but little from her own? / Where is she? And how doth she? And what says / My conceal'd lady to our cancell'd love?

Were you talking about Juliet? How is she? Doesn't she think I'm a hardened murderer, now that I've stained the childhood of our happiness with blood so closely related to her own? Where is she? And how is she? And what does my secret wife say about our cancelled love?
O, she says nothing, sir, but weeps and weeps; / And now falls on her bed, and then starts up, / And Tybalt calls, and then on Romeo cries, / And then down falls again.
Oh, she says nothing, sir, but weeps and weeps. One moment she falls on her bed, the next she jumps up and calls out 'Tybalt', and then cries out 'Romeo', and then falls down again.

As if that name, / Shot from the deadly level of a gun, / Did murder her, as that name's cursed hand / Murder'd her kinsman. O, tell me, Friar, tell me, / In what vile part of this anatomy / Doth my name lodge? Tell me, that I may sack / The hateful mansion.

As if that name, fired from the deadly aim of a gun, murdered her, just as that name's cursed hand murdered her cousin. Oh, tell me, Friar, tell me, in what vile part of this body does my name live? Tell me, so that I can destroy that hateful house.

Hold thy desperate hand. / Art thou a man? Thy form cries out thou art. / Thy tears are womanish, thy wild acts denote / The unreasonable fury of a beast. / Unseemly woman in a seeming man, / And ill-beseeming beast in seeming both! / Thou hast amaz'd me. By my holy order, / I thought thy disposition better temper'd. / Hast thou slain Tybalt? Wilt thou slay thyself? / And slay thy lady, that in thy life lives, / By doing damned hate upon thyself? / Why rail'st thou on thy birth, the heaven and earth? / Since birth, and heaven and earth, all three do meet / In thee at once; which thou at once wouldst lose. / Fie, fie, thou sham'st thy shape, thy love, thy wit, / Which, like a usurer, abound'st in all, / And usest none in that true use indeed / Which should bedeck thy shape, thy love, thy wit. / Thy noble shape is but a form of wax, / Digressing from the valour of a man; / Thy dear love sworn but hollow perjury, / Killing that love which thou hast vow'd to cherish; / Thy wit, that ornament to shape and love, / Misshapen in the conduct of them both, / Like powder in a skilless soldier's flask, / Is set afire by thine own ignorance, / And thou dismember'd with thine own defence. / What, rouse thee, man. Thy Juliet is alive, / For whose dear sake thou wast but lately dead. / There art thou happy. Tybalt would kill thee, / But thou slew'st Tybalt; there art thou happy. / The law that threaten'd death becomes thy friend, / And turns it to exile; there art thou happy. / A pack of blessings light upon thy back; / Happiness courts thee in her best array; / But like a misshaped and sullen wench, / Thou putt'st up thy Fortune and thy love. / Take heed, take heed, for such die miserable. / Go, get thee to thy love as was decreed, / Ascend her chamber, hence and comfort her. / But look thou stay not till the watch be set, / For then thou canst not pass to Mantua; / Where thou shalt live till we can find a time / To blaze your marriage, reconcile your friends, / Beg pardon of the Prince, and call thee back / With twenty hundred thousand times more joy / Than thou went'st forth in lamentation. / Go before, Nurse. Commend me to thy lady, / And bid her hasten all the house to bed, / Which heavy sorrow makes them apt unto. / Romeo is coming.

Stop your desperate hand! Are you a man? Your body shouts that you are, but your tears are womanish, and your wild actions show the irrational fury of a beast. You're an ugly woman disguised as a man, and an unnatural beast disguised as both! You've amazed me. By my holy order, I thought your character was better balanced. Have you killed Tybalt? Will you kill yourself, and kill your lady, who lives through your life, by doing a damned act of hatred against yourself? Why do you curse your birth, and heaven and earth, when birth, heaven and earth all meet in you at once, and you would throw all three away at once? Shame, shame! You disgrace your body, your love and your intelligence. Like a moneylender, you have plenty of all of them and use none of them as they should be used, to do credit to your body, your love and your intelligence. Your noble body is only a wax model if it turns away from a man's courage. Your dear sworn love is only an empty lie if you kill the love you vowed to cherish. Your intelligence, which should adorn your body and your love, is misused in guiding them both, and like gunpowder in a clumsy soldier's flask, it's set on fire by your own ignorance, and you're blown apart by the very thing that should defend you. Come on, wake up, man! Your Juliet is alive, for whose dear sake you were dead just now: you're lucky there. Tybalt would have killed you, but you killed Tybalt: you're lucky there. The law that threatened death has become your friend and changed it to exile: you're lucky there. A whole pack of blessings lands on your back. Happiness courts you in her finest clothes. But like a badly behaved, sulky girl, you pout at your good fortune and your love. Be careful, be careful, because people like that die miserable. Go, go to your love as was arranged. Climb up to her room, go and comfort her. But make sure you don't stay until the night watch is posted, because then you won't be able to get through to Mantua. You'll live there until we can find the right time to announce your marriage, reconcile your families, beg the Prince's pardon and call you back with two million times more joy than you had grief when you left.
