Saint Francis help me! How often tonight have my old feet stumbled over graves! Who's there? Who's keeping company with the dead so late?
Here's one, a friend, and one that knows you well.
It's a friend, and one who knows you well.
Bliss be upon you. Tell me, good my friend, / What torch is yond that vainly lends his light / To grubs and eyeless skulls? As I discern, / It burneth in the Capels' monument.
Bless you! Tell me, my good friend, what's that torch over there giving its light uselessly to worms and eyeless skulls? As far as I can see, it's burning in the Capulets' tomb.
It doth so, holy sir, and there's my master, / One that you love.
It is, holy sir, and my master is there, someone you love.
How long hath he been there?
How long has he been there?
Go with me to the vault.
Come with me to the vault.
I dare not, sir; / My master knows not but I am gone hence, / And fearfully did menace me with death / If I did stay to look on his intents.
I don't dare, sir. My master thinks I've gone, and he threatened me fiercely with death if I stayed to watch what he meant to do.
Stay then, I'll go alone. Fear comes upon me. / O, much I fear some ill unlucky thing.
Stay, then. I'll go alone. Fear is coming over me. Oh, I'm very afraid something bad and unlucky has happened.
As I did sleep under this yew tree here, / I dreamt my master and another fought, / And that my master slew him.
As I was sleeping under this yew tree, I dreamt that my master and another man fought, and that my master killed him.
Romeo! [Advances] / Alack, alack, what blood is this which stains / The stony entrance of this sepulchre? / What mean these masterless and gory swords / To lie discolour'd by this place of peace?
Romeo! Oh no, oh no, whose blood is this staining the stone entrance of this tomb? What are these bloody swords doing, without their owners, lying stained by this place of peace?
Romeo! O, pale! Who else? What, Paris too? / And steep'd in blood? Ah what an unkind hour / Is guilty of this lamentable chance? / The lady stirs.
Romeo! Oh, so pale! Who else? What, Paris too? And soaked in blood? Ah, what cruel hour is guilty of this terrible event? The lady is stirring.
O comfortable Friar, where is my lord? / I do remember well where I should be, / And there I am. Where is my Romeo?
Oh, comforting Friar, where is my husband? I remember clearly where I should be, and here I am. Where is my Romeo?

I hear some noise. Lady, come from that nest / Of death, contagion, and unnatural sleep. / A greater power than we can contradict / Hath thwarted our intents. Come, come away. / Thy husband in thy bosom there lies dead; / And Paris too. Come, I'll dispose of thee / Among a sisterhood of holy nuns. / Stay not to question, for the watch is coming. / Come, go, good Juliet. I dare no longer stay.

I hear a noise. Lady, come out of that nest of death, disease and unnatural sleep. A greater power than we can oppose has spoiled our plans. Come, come away. Your husband lies dead there on your breast, and Paris too. Come, I'll place you in a sisterhood of holy nuns. Don't stop to ask questions, because the watch is coming. Come on, go, good Juliet. I don't dare stay any longer.
Go, get thee hence, for I will not away.
Go, get away, because I won't leave.

What's here? A cup clos'd in my true love's hand? / Poison, I see, hath been his timeless end. / O churl. Drink all, and left no friendly drop / To help me after? I will kiss thy lips. / Haply some poison yet doth hang on them, / To make me die with a restorative.

What's this? A cup clasped in my true love's hand? I see poison has been his untimely end. Oh, you miser! You drank it all and left no friendly drop to help me follow you? I'll kiss your lips. Perhaps some poison still hangs on them, to make me die with a medicine that restores me to you.
Lead the way, boy. Which way?
Yea, noise? Then I'll be brief. O happy dagger.
What, a noise? Then I'll be quick. Oh, lucky dagger!
This is thy sheath. [Stabs herself] There rest, and let me die.
This is your sheath. Rest there, and let me die.
This is the place. There, where the torch doth burn.
This is the place. There, where the torch is burning.
The ground is bloody. Search about the churchyard. / Go, some of you, whoe'er you find attach.
The ground is bloody. Search the churchyard. Go, some of you, and arrest whoever you find.

Pitiful sight! Here lies the County slain, / And Juliet bleeding, warm, and newly dead, / Who here hath lain this two days buried. / Go tell the Prince; run to the Capulets. / Raise up the Montagues, some others search.

A pitiful sight! Here lies the Count, killed, and Juliet bleeding, warm and just dead, who has been lying here buried for two days. Go and tell the Prince. Run to the Capulets. Wake up the Montagues. Some of you others, search.
We see the ground whereon these woes do lie, / But the true ground of all these piteous woes / We cannot without circumstance descry.
We can see the ground on which these sad bodies lie, but we can't discover the true grounds, the cause, of all these pitiful sorrows without more details.
Here's Romeo's man. We found him in the churchyard.
Here's Romeo's servant. We found him in the churchyard.
Hold him in safety till the Prince come hither.
Keep him under guard until the Prince gets here.
Here is a Friar that trembles, sighs, and weeps. / We took this mattock and this spade from him / As he was coming from this churchyard side.
Here's a friar who is trembling, sighing and weeping. We took this pickaxe and spade from him as he was coming from this side of the churchyard.
A great suspicion. Stay the Friar too.
Very suspicious. Hold the friar too.
What misadventure is so early up, / That calls our person from our morning's rest?
What disaster has happened so early that it calls me from my morning rest?
What should it be that they so shriek abroad?
What can it be that they're shrieking about out there?
O the people in the street cry Romeo, / Some Juliet, and some Paris, and all run / With open outcry toward our monument.
Oh, the people in the street are crying 'Romeo', some 'Juliet' and some 'Paris', and all are running, shouting out loud, towards our tomb.
What fear is this which startles in our ears?
What is this fear that's ringing in our ears?
Sovereign, here lies the County Paris slain, / And Romeo dead, and Juliet, dead before, / Warm and new kill'd.
Your Highness, here lies Count Paris, killed, and Romeo dead, and Juliet, who was dead before, warm and newly killed.
Search, seek, and know how this foul murder comes.
Search, look and find out how this foul murder happened.
Here is a Friar, and slaughter'd Romeo's man, / With instruments upon them fit to open / These dead men's tombs.
Here's a friar, and the dead Romeo's servant, with tools on them suitable for opening these dead men's tombs.
O heaven! O wife, look how our daughter bleeds! / This dagger hath mista'en, for lo, his house / Is empty on the back of Montague, / And it mis-sheathed in my daughter's bosom.
Oh heaven! Oh wife, look how our daughter is bleeding! This dagger has gone to the wrong place: look, its sheath is empty on Montague's back, and it's sheathed wrongly in my daughter's breast.
O me! This sight of death is as a bell / That warns my old age to a sepulchre.
Oh no! This sight of death is like a bell calling me in my old age to the grave.
Come, Montague, for thou art early up, / To see thy son and heir more early down.
Come, Montague. You're up early to see your son and heir even earlier laid down.
Alas, my liege, my wife is dead tonight. / Grief of my son's exile hath stopp'd her breath. / What further woe conspires against mine age?
Alas, my lord, my wife died tonight. Grief at my son's exile stopped her breath. What further misery is plotting against me in my old age?
O thou untaught! What manners is in this, / To press before thy father to a grave?
Oh, you badly brought up boy! What kind of manners is this, to push ahead of your father into a grave?

Seal up the mouth of outrage for a while, / Till we can clear these ambiguities, / And know their spring, their head, their true descent, / And then will I be general of your woes, / And lead you even to death. Meantime forbear, / And let mischance be slave to patience. / Bring forth the parties of suspicion.

Stop your cries of outrage for a while, until we can clear up these mysteries and know their source, their beginning and how they came about. Then I'll lead you in your grief, even to death. Meanwhile be patient, and let misfortune be ruled by patience. Bring out the people under suspicion.

I am the greatest, able to do least, / Yet most suspected, as the time and place / Doth make against me, of this direful murder. / And here I stand, both to impeach and purge / Myself condemned and myself excus'd.

I am the most suspected, though the least able to have done it, since the time and place are against me, of this dreadful murder. And here I stand, both to accuse and to clear myself, condemned by myself and excused by myself.
Then say at once what thou dost know in this.
Then say at once what you know about this.

I will be brief, for my short date of breath / Is not so long as is a tedious tale. / Romeo, there dead, was husband to that Juliet, / And she, there dead, that Romeo's faithful wife. / I married them; and their stol'n marriage day / Was Tybalt's doomsday, whose untimely death / Banish'd the new-made bridegroom from this city; / For whom, and not for Tybalt, Juliet pin'd. / You, to remove that siege of grief from her, / Betroth'd, and would have married her perforce / To County Paris. Then comes she to me, / And with wild looks, bid me devise some means / To rid her from this second marriage, / Or in my cell there would she kill herself. / Then gave I her, so tutored by my art, / A sleeping potion, which so took effect / As I intended, for it wrought on her / The form of death. Meantime I writ to Romeo / That he should hither come as this dire night / To help to take her from her borrow'd grave, / Being the time the potion's force should cease. / But he which bore my letter, Friar John, / Was stay'd by accident; and yesternight / Return'd my letter back. Then all alone / At the prefixed hour of her waking / Came I to take her from her kindred's vault, / Meaning to keep her closely at my cell / Till I conveniently could send to Romeo. / But when I came, some minute ere the time / Of her awaking, here untimely lay / The noble Paris and true Romeo dead. / She wakes; and I entreated her come forth / And bear this work of heaven with patience. / But then a noise did scare me from the tomb; / And she, too desperate, would not go with me, / But, as it seems, did violence on herself. / All this I know; and to the marriage / Her Nurse is privy. And if ought in this / Miscarried by my fault, let my old life / Be sacrific'd, some hour before his time, / Unto the rigour of severest law.

I'll be brief, because the short time I have left to live isn't as long as a tedious story. Romeo, dead there, was husband to that Juliet, and she, dead there, was Romeo's faithful wife. I married them, and their secret wedding day was the day Tybalt died, whose early death banished the new bridegroom from this city. It was for him, not for Tybalt, that Juliet was pining. To lift that siege of grief from her, you engaged her and would have married her by force to Count Paris. Then she came to me, with wild looks, and told me to find some way to rid her of this second marriage, or she would kill herself there in my cell. So I gave her a sleeping potion, made by my skill, which worked as I intended, because it gave her the appearance of death. Meanwhile I wrote to Romeo telling him to come here on this dreadful night to help take her from her borrowed grave, since this was when the potion's effect would end. But the man who carried my letter, Friar John, was held up by accident, and last night he brought my letter back. Then, all alone, at the hour fixed for her waking, I came to take her from her family's vault, meaning to hide her at my cell until I could send for Romeo. But when I came, some minutes before she woke, the noble Paris and faithful Romeo lay here dead before their time. She woke, and I begged her to come out and bear this act of heaven with patience. But then a noise frightened me out of the tomb, and she, too desperate, wouldn't come with me, but, it seems, did violence to herself. This is all I know, and her Nurse knows about the marriage. And if any part of this went wrong through my fault, let my old life be sacrificed, a few hours before its natural end, to the full severity of the law.
We still have known thee for a holy man. / Where's Romeo's man? What can he say to this?
We've always known you to be a holy man. Where is Romeo's servant? What can he say about this?

I brought my master news of Juliet's death, / And then in post he came from Mantua / To this same place, to this same monument. / This letter he early bid me give his father, / And threaten'd me with death, going in the vault, / If I departed not, and left him there.

I brought my master news of Juliet's death, and then he rode at full speed from Mantua to this same place, this same tomb. He told me to give this letter to his father early, and as he went into the vault, he threatened me with death if I didn't go away and leave him there.
Give me the letter, I will look on it. / Where is the County's Page that rais'd the watch? / Sirrah, what made your master in this place?
Give me the letter. I'll look at it. Where is the Count's page, who called the watch? Boy, what was your master doing in this place?

He came with flowers to strew his lady's grave, / And bid me stand aloof, and so I did. / Anon comes one with light to ope the tomb, / And by and by my master drew on him, / And then I ran away to call the watch.

He came with flowers to scatter on his lady's grave, and told me to stand at a distance, and I did. Soon someone came with a light to open the tomb, and before long my master drew his sword on him, and then I ran away to call the watch.

This letter doth make good the Friar's words, / Their course of love, the tidings of her death. / And here he writes that he did buy a poison / Of a poor 'pothecary, and therewithal / Came to this vault to die, and lie with Juliet. / Where be these enemies? Capulet, Montague, / See what a scourge is laid upon your hate, / That heaven finds means to kill your joys with love! / And I, for winking at your discords too, / Have lost a brace of kinsmen. All are punish'd.

This letter confirms the Friar's words: the course of their love and the news of her death. And here he writes that he bought a poison from a poor apothecary, and with it came to this vault to die and lie with Juliet. Where are these enemies? Capulet, Montague, see what a punishment has been laid on your hatred, that heaven finds ways to kill your joys with love! And I, for turning a blind eye to your quarrels, have lost two relatives. Everyone is punished.
O brother Montague, give me thy hand. / This is my daughter's jointure, for no more / Can I demand.
Oh brother Montague, give me your hand. This is my daughter's marriage settlement, because I can't ask for anything more.
But I can give thee more, / For I will raise her statue in pure gold, / That whiles Verona by that name is known, / There shall no figure at such rate be set / As that of true and faithful Juliet.
But I can give you more, because I'll raise a statue of her in pure gold, so that as long as Verona is known by that name, no statue will be valued as highly as that of true and faithful Juliet.
As rich shall Romeo's by his lady's lie, / Poor sacrifices of our enmity.
Romeo's statue will lie just as richly beside his lady's: poor sacrifices to our hatred!

A glooming peace this morning with it brings; / The sun for sorrow will not show his head. / Go hence, to have more talk of these sad things. / Some shall be pardon'd, and some punished, / For never was a story of more woe / Than this of Juliet and her Romeo.

This morning brings a gloomy peace with it. The sun won't show its face for sorrow. Go away and talk more about these sad things. Some will be pardoned, and some punished, because there was never a story of more misery than this one of Juliet and her Romeo.
